IX. A Reminder of How to Live as New Human Beings (4:17–5:2)

A. No Longer Walk as “Gentiles” but as a New Human Being (4:17–24)

B. Living as Human Beings Newly Created in God’s Image (4:25–5:2)


B. Living as Human Beings Newly Created in God’s Image (4:25–5:2)

Paul now begins to give practical advice on how his readers can live out the new existence he has just described in 4:20–24. The “therefore” with which the section begins probably connects these specific admonitions not only to the whole concept of taking off the old human being and putting on the new human being, but especially to the idea articulated in 4:24 that the newly donned human being is created in the image of God. The admonitions in 4:25–5:2, then, are practical illustrations of what it means to live as a new creature, made in God’s image, and no longer under the sway of the old human being.

This idea of living as a creature in God’s image reemerges at the end of the passage in 5:1–2, a section that looks back over the admonitions just given and offers a summary statement of their implications. “So,” Paul says, “be imitators of God.” To imitate God, he continues, means to live in love, and the supreme example of the kind of love that God exercises is Christ’s willingness to atone for the sins of others by means of his sacrificial death.

The specific, practical admonitions in 4:25–32 are sandwiched between the reference to believers as created in God’s image and the summary statement that they should be imitators of God’s love. They illustrate the meaning, then, of living out one’s new existence as a re-created human being in relationship with others.

These admonitions exhibit the same mixture of rhetorical order and disorder that appears elsewhere in the letter. The four admonitions in 4:25, 28, 29, and 31–32 show an unmistakable pattern: an admonition not to do something (lie, steal, use foul language, and angrily abuse people) is followed by a matching positive admonition to do something (tell the truth, work hard for what is good, use edifying speech, and forgive) and then a motivating reason for following the admonition (we are members of each other, to help the needy, to give grace to the hearer, because Christ forgave others). The admonition in 4:26–27, however, follows the pattern only in rough terms: a positive command is followed by three negative commands, the last of which probably supplies a motivation for the previous admonitions, but does so rather indirectly: “Do not . . . give place to the devil.” The admonition in 4:30, moreover, probably supplies a second motivation for avoiding foul speech (not avoiding this grieves God’s Holy Spirit), but it is phrased in the imperative mood, as if it functions as a separate exhortation (cf. v. 27).

In addition to these irregularities, there is a rhetorical imbalance in the attention given to the subjects addressed. Most of the admonitions concern speech, especially if we remember that in antiquity the verb ὀργίζομαι (orgizomai; v. 26) and the noun ὀργή (orgē; v. 31) described the open and often-violent expression of what we call anger today (W. V. Harris 2001: 50–70). Lying, screaming in rage, foul talk, and slander, then, consume much of the paragraph. By comparison, the admonitions about stealing and grieving the Holy Spirit are brief.

The combination of order and disorder in this section point both to the extemporary nature of the discourse and to its exemplary function. These admonitions were composed on the spot and give examples of what it means to live as a new human being who reflects the image of its Creator and imitates the quality of his love.



Exegesis and Exposition

4:25Therefore, put off falsehood and speak the truth—each of you—with his or her neighbor because we are members of one another.

26Be angry, and do not sin. Do not let the sun set on your wrath, 27nor give place to the devil.

28Let the one who steals steal no longer, but rather let him labor by working ⌜what is good with his own hands⌝ that he might have something to share with the one who has need.

29Let no rotten speech come out of your mouth, but if there is anything good [let it come out of your mouth] for building up ⌜where the need exists⌝ that it might give grace to those who hear.

30And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.

31Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and yelling be removed from among you, with all mean-spiritedness. 32But be kind to one another, compassionate, forgiving each other, just as God also forgave ⌜us⌝ in Christ.

5:1So, then, be ⌜imitators of God⌝ as beloved children, 2and walk in love, just as Christ loved ⌜us⌝ and gave himself ⌜for us, an offering and sacrifice⌝ to God, for a fragrant aroma.

[4:25] Most commentators think that the particle διό (dio, therefore) refers back to the entire previous paragraph and that Paul here gives specific examples of how his readers should live since their experience of the conversion described there. Διό, however, can refer back to the immediately preceding statement about the new human being’s creation in the image of God (v. 24; cf. the use of διό in 4:8 and 5:14); since Paul summarizes his specific instructions in 4:25–32 with the admonition “So, then, be imitators of God” (5:1), it seems likely that διό points back primarily (although not solely) to 4:24, where the image-of-God theme is articulated as a motivation for ethics (cf. Lincoln 1990: 300). In what follows, Paul will give concrete examples from everyday life of what it means to live out the new life he has just described in 4:22–24, but especially the new reality of re-creation in the image of God.

This is the first of four admonitions in 4:25–5:2 that take first a negative form, then a positive form, and then supply a clause giving the reason for the admonition (cf. vv. 25, 28, 29, and 31). Here Paul gives a negative exhortation not to lie, then a positive command to speak the truth, and finally a clause indicating why truthfulness with each other is important.

The negative part of the admonition uses an aorist participle of ἀποτίθημι (apotithēmi, put off) and urges Paul’s readers to put off “falsehood” (τὸ ψεῦδος, to pseudos).[1] This language recalls the figure from 4:22 of putting off the clothing of the old human being that “deceit” (ἀπάτη, apatē) was busily corrupting, and provides a concrete example of how the old human being manifests itself in day-to-day life: telling lies is perhaps the most obvious vice of a former way of life whose chief characteristic was deceit.

It is perhaps not accidental that Paul used the expression τὸ ψεῦδος (to pseudos, a lie) in Rom. 1:25 to say that Gentile idolatry exchanges the truth about God for falsehood. Here too he may be thinking not merely of lying in general (cf. Col. 3:9) but also of the kind of theological falsehood concerning the divine that filled Gentile religion, the kind of religious lying that eventually leads to the human disorientation and despair described in 4:17–19 (and in Rom. 1:18–32).

Paul next articulates the same admonition in positive terms. His language is so close to Zech. 8:16 LXX that there must be some connection:

Zechariah 8:16 LXX Ephesians 4:25



* * *





λαλεῖτε ἀλήθειαν ἕκαστος πρὸς τὸν πλησίον αὐτοῦ λαλεῖτε ἀλήθειαν ἕκαστος μετὰ τοῦ πλησίον αὐτοῦ



* * *





laleite alētheian hekastos pros ton plēsion autou laleite alētheian hekastos meta tou plēsion autou



* * *





speak the truth—each of you—to his [or her] neighbor speak the truth—each of you—with his [or her] neighbor



* * *





The only difference is the exchange of μετά (meta, with) for πρός (pros, to) and then the necessary change in the case of the article. Both statements have basically the same meaning.

To what extent this literary connection between the two texts also implies thematic connections is unclear. Some interpreters have argued that Eph. 4 and Zech. 8 are woven together at a “profound salvation-historical and typological” level (O’Brien 1999: 337). Zechariah 8 promises that God will restore the fortunes of Jerusalem for the remnant of his people after the difficult days during which God had punished them for their refusal to listen to him. After describing the idyllic scene of the restored Jerusalem, the Lord issues several ethical admonitions to his people, the first of which is to speak truthfully to each other—the text whose language reappears here in Eph. 4:25. Zechariah 8 ends with a promise that the nations will one day converge on Jerusalem to seek the Lord’s favor (Pokorný 1992: 191). The use of Zech. 8:16 here, then, implies that Paul (or the author) considers his readers to be God’s newly created humanity and the fulfillment of these promises:

What is predicated of the eschatological future of God’s people in terms of new Jerusalem language in the OT passage is picked up by Paul in relation to the “new person,” God’s new community in Christ, upon whom the ends of the ages have come. The salvation-historical and typological connections between the two communities, and thus the accompanying practical exhortations, are patent. (O’Brien 1999: 338)

Others have not taken the correspondence this far but believe that the close correspondence between the language of the two passages (Moritz 1996a: 889) or the similar structure of the ethical admonitions in Eph. 4:25–30 to Zech. 8:16–17 (Sampley 1972: 107–8) at least show that the author was aware he was quoting the OT.

On the other side stand those who think that the author of Ephesians simply took over a traditional sequence of ethical exhortations that had already absorbed the language of Zech. 8:16. These interpreters point to the coupling of anger with deceit in Jewish literature devoted to ethical instruction (e.g., T. Dan 1.3; 2.1–2, 4; 3.5–6; 4.7; 6.8) and to allusions to Zech. 8:16 in admonitions not to lie in this same literature (T. Reu. 6.9; T. Dan 5.2; T. Benj. 10.3). They point out the close parallel to Eph. 4:25–26 in T. Dan 4.7–5.2, where an admonition to beware of anger is followed by an admonition not to lie, and this is backed up by a clear allusion to Zech. 8:16.[2] Such parallels, the argument goes, make it likely that the author of Ephesians has simply taken over Zech. 8:16 from traditional Hellenistic Jewish ethical exhortation.

Perhaps the best way forward is to recognize that Paul probably found the reference to Zech. 8:16 in the tradition but, even so, both recognized Zechariah as the source of this traditional language and knew the broader context in Zechariah from which the language came.[3] Since he drew no theological implications from the wider context, it remains unclear whether he expected his Gentile readers to pick up detailed echoes of Zech. 8 in this language. He may simply have left the matter open, recognizing that the language could be understood on a deeper level by those who were able to do so, but believing that it was not critical for his basic meaning that his readers be able to do this.

Last, Paul provides a motivation for putting off “lying” and speaking truth to one’s neighbor: “we are members [μέλη, melē] of one another” (cf. Rom. 12:5; 1 Clem. 47.7). This recalls Eph. 4:15–16, where speaking the truth in love is the antidote to the trickery of false teaching, and each “part” (μέρος, meros) of the body plays a role in helping the body grow to maturity. Although any lying within the body of Christ would be covered by this admonition, Paul may have been thinking especially of theological lying—the sort of false teaching about God that leads to the bleak existence of unbelievers described in 4:17–19 and that can even lead believers astray (cf. Jude 4; 2 Pet. 2:2, 18; Thielman 2005: 512–16, 522–27, 652–55).

[4:26–27] Paul next forbids his readers from allowing anger to fester since doing so gives the devil an opportunity to advance his strategies (cf. 6:11). The set of imperatives, one positive and one negative, repeats the wording of Ps. 4:5 LXX, MT (4:4, Eng.) exactly: ὀργίζεσθε καὶ μὴ ἁμαρτάνετε (orgizesthe kai mē hamartanete, be angry, and do not sin).[4] The psalmist (Ps. 4:3 LXX, MT [4:2 Eng.]) directs these imperatives to his enemies, important people who have sullied his reputation with “empty” words (ματαιότητα, mataiotēta; cf. Eph. 4:17) and “lying” (ψεῦδος, pseudos; cf. Eph. 4:25).[5] In this context, the command “Be angry and do not sin” could be paraphrased, “Be angry if you must, but stop sinning by continuing your empty, false speech.” This seems to be Paul’s meaning also, although there is some debate about this.

Some interpreters believe Paul’s first imperative (ὀργίζεσθε) implies that in some settings anger is not only appropriate but also necessary. Paul is, then, both instructing his readers to show this appropriate anger and urging them to deal with the cause of this anger quickly (Wallace 1989; 1996: 491–92; cf. Hoehner 2002: 620–21). On the side of this interpretation lies the coordinating conjunction καί (kai, and), which on this reading performs its usual function of linking two syntactically equal elements: a command to be angry and a command not to sin. Paul could have used a participial form of ὀργίζω (orgizō) if he had intended to give this verb a conditional or concessive nuance (“If you are angry . . .” or “Although you are angry . . .”).

This consideration is outweighed, however, by the emphasis the context places on the second imperative in this two-imperative couplet (“Be angry and do not sin”). The next two imperatives, like the second member of the couplet, are prohibitions (“Do not let the sun set on your wrath, nor give place to the devil”). The context, then, is concerned with avoiding sin in situations where anger is present. This makes it likely that the first, positive imperative in the whole series is simply intended to set the stage for the prohibitions that follow.

Whether the anger is justified seems to be outside the purview of the admonition. Where anger is present, Paul says, a potentially sinful situation exists. Those who are angry should recognize this and take practical steps to avoid sinning.

Paul expresses no interest in the philosophical debate current in his time over whether all anger is harmful and should be eliminated or some anger is justified and people should seek to channel it in useful directions (W. V. Harris 2001: 102–4, 110–20).[6] Here he views anger simply as an emotion that can quickly become sinful. This conclusion is consistent with the findings of W. V. Harris’s careful study (2001: 63) of the terminology of anger in classical antiquity:

I suggest that all or most of what was thought of in the period, say, 450 B.C. to 300 A.D. as orgē-anger and thumos-anger was by modern standards quite furious and intense, though some of it was long-lived. A corollary might be that a good deal of what we regard as anger was either referred to by milder terms, such as chalepotēs, or even considered too trivial to be attended to or mentioned.

If Paul is thinking of what by modern standards would be intense anger, his next statement offers practical advice to keep this emotion from becoming long-lived and reaching the crescendo of verbal abuse described in 4:31. Those who are angry, he says, should not let the sun set on their παροργισμός (parorgismos, wrath). This term is rare, appearing prior to its use here only in the LXX, where it most often refers to the provocation of anger (1 Kings 15:30; 2 Kings 23:26; Neh. 9:18, 26 [2 Esd. 19:18, 26 LXX]; Pss. Sol. 8.9), although it can refer to anger itself (2 Kings 19:3; Jer. 21:5). Here the word probably serves as a synonym for ὀργή (orgē), perhaps with a hint, supplied by the prefix παρά (para), that as time passes, unattended anger is likely to increase. The wisdom here is proverbial, as the frequently cited parallels in both Greek and Hebrew literature show (Plutarch, Frat. amor. 488b–c; 1QS 5.26–6.1; CD-A 7.2–3; 9.6–8). “Alas for those who devise wickedness and evil deeds on their beds!” Micah says. “When the morning dawns, they perform it, because it is in their power” (2:1 NRSV; cf. Ps. 36:4).

The next prohibition (v. 27) provides the reason why it is unwise to let one’s anger fester: doing so gives τόπον τῷ διαβόλῳ (topon tō diabolō, place to the devil). The expression “to give place to” (διδόναι τόπον τινί, didonai topon tini) was a common Greek idiom for giving someone or something an opportunity (e.g., Rom. 12:19; Sir. 4:5; Wis. 12:10; Plutarch, Cohib. ira 14; BDAG 1012; Jewett 2007: 775). The later Pauline letters depict the devil as a schemer (Eph. 6:11) who entraps people (1 Tim. 3:7; 2 Tim. 2:26), and so here the thought is probably of the devil taking the opportunity offered by long-term anger to encourage the kind of mischief listed in Eph. 4:31: “bitterness and rage and anger and yelling and slander . . . with all mean-spiritedness.”

[4:28] Paul next urges his audience not to steal. As with the first admonition in 4:25, this one follows the pattern of a negative command (“Let the one who steals steal no longer”) followed by its positive counterpart (“but rather let him labor by working what is good with his own hands”) and a motivating reason for engaging in the behavior (“that he might have something to share with the one who has need”).

Ancient Greeks and Romans commonly assumed that stealing (κλέπτειν, kleptein) was wrong (e.g., Plato, Resp. 1.344; Arius Didymus 10e, 11e [Pomeroy 1999: 62–63, 68–69]; Epictetus [Arrian, Epict. diss. 1.9.15, 17]; Deissmann 1978: 316n6), and the exhortation not to steal features prominently in the OT (Exod. 20:15; 22:1; Deut. 5:19; Lev. 19:11; Jer. 7:9; Hos. 4:2) and Judaism (e.g., Ps.-Phoc. 6, 18, 135–36, 153–54 [W. Wilson 2005: 180]; Philo, Spec. Laws 4.1–40). It is frequently repeated in early Christian literature in various forms: in summaries of the Decalogue (Rom. 13:9; Mark 10:19; Matt. 19:18; Luke 18:20), in lists of vices (1 Cor. 6:10; 1 Pet. 4:15; cf. Rom. 2:21), and, as here, in general moral exhortation (Did. 3.5; 1 Clem. 36.8).

The verb κλέπτω (kleptō) and its corresponding noun κλέπτης (kleptēs, thief) refer to stealing secretly rather than to violent robbery (Preisker, TDNT 3:754). Paul probably has in mind, then, the working poor whose income would fluctuate with the seasons in the agrarian economy of Roman Asia and who may have supplemented their income in difficult times by secretly stealing from their employers and others (Best 1997a: 182–83). He is not thinking of slaves, since Paul admonishes his readers to stop stealing and earn their income (Best 1997a: 182). He is also not thinking of the wealthy since the recipients of this command are to earn their income by hard manual labor (κοπιάτω ἐργαζόμενος ταῖς ἰδίαις χερσίν, kopiatō ergazomenos tais idiais chersin, let him labor by working with his own hands).

Rather than stealing, the thief is to be engaged in “working what is good” (ἐργαζόμενος . . . τὸ ἀγαθόν, ergazomenos . . . to agathon), a reference to work that is helpful and beneficial to others (cf. Gal. 6:10). Paul’s Christian readers should employ their hands in honest labor that benefits others, presumably their employer. Best (1997a: 181–83) has persuasively argued that this admonition reveals something about the social class of the letter’s first audience: it at least included people so poor that they were tempted to steal and could be admonished to earn their own living by hard manual labor.

The purpose clause that concludes the admonition states the reason why honest labor for the benefit of others is important. By working hard, those who labor will “have something to share with the one who has need.” To describe the motivation for work in terms of giving to the needy may seem surprisingly sweeping, but this sentiment is not unique within early Christian literature (cf. Acts 20:35; Titus 3:14; Did. 4.6). It is also in step with other similarly emphatic statements in the NT about care for the needy (1 Tim. 5:8; James 1:27; 1 John 3:17). Meeting the needs of the Christian poor was one of the characteristic features of the early Christian movement.[7]

[4:29] Paul next turns to speech, and the now-familiar threefold pattern reappears: Paul’s audience should engage in

no rotten speech (negative),

but instead in edifying speech (positive),

that it may give grace to the hearer (motivation).

Paul begins by forbidding all σαπρός (sapros) speech. Used literally, this term could refer to “rancid” fish, “rotten” wood, “withered” flowers, “diseased” lungs (LSJ 1583) or the “putrid” smell that accompanied the hideous figure of personified Death (T. Ab. 16.4 and 17.8 [rec. A]; cf. 13.1–14.9 [rec. B]).[8] In the NT, it refers to “bad” trees that produce “bad” fruit (Matt. 7:17–18; 12:33) or to the useless “junk” (τὰ . . . σαπρά, ta . . . sapra) that fishermen pull out of the water in their seine nets and separate from “the good stuff” (τὰ καλά, ta kala; Matt. 13:48; BDAG 913). Used figuratively, the term could mean “bad, evil, unwholesome” (BDAG 913). It is possible that Paul is thinking of sexually crude speech (cf. 5:4; Col. 3:8; Lincoln 1990: 305; Muddiman 2001: 228), but since the opposite of σαπρός is “something good [ἀγαθός, agathos] for building up [οἰκοδομή, oikodomē],” he is probably thinking more generally of any speech that works against “the building up [οἰκοδομή] of the body of Christ” (4:12). Σαπρός speech would then be speech that was not merely “ugly” but also “useless.” This would cover not only the sexually crude, foolish speech of 5:4 but also the theologically deceptive speech of 4:14.﻿[9]

In contrast to σαπρός speech, Paul exhorts his readers to engage in speech that is genuine, substantive, and actually accomplishes something of benefit to the Christian community. This seems to be the meaning of the phrase “something good [ἀγαθός] for building up [οἰκοδομή].” Paul has just used the term ἀγαθός to contrast the good that honest work accomplishes with the harm that comes from stealing (4:28), and it is likely that ἀγαθός carries the same nuance of what is “beneficial” here. Since Paul has used the language of edification in the letter up to this point to refer to building up the community of believers, the term οἰκοδομή gives the idea of laboring for what is beneficial a decidedly communal tilt (2:20–22; 4:12, 16).

The genitive phrase τῆς χρείας (tēs chreias), which qualifies the noun οἰκοδομή, is difficult. What could “the building up of the need” mean? Clearly it does not mean what it seems to mean when taken literally (encouraging or increasing need) but the opposite of this. An early scribe or translator in the Western tradition could apparently make no sense of the phrase and substituted πίστεως in place of χρείας to yield the more intelligible idea that Christian speech should “build up the faith” (see the additional note). Jerome understood πρὸς οἰκοδομὴν τῆς χρείας (pros oikodomēn tēs chreias) to mean “for the building up of the occasion,” which he explained as a reference to speaking what was edifying as the occasion arose (Heine 2002: 198–99). Others have taken τῆς χρείας as a qualitative genitive (“needed upbuilding”; e.g., Barth 1974: 519; Lincoln 1990: 306) or a genitive of reference (“upbuilding with reference to the need”; e.g., De Wette 1843: 144; Ellicott 1859: 108–9).

There is a parallel to this expression in the first-century Testament of Job that both shows the expression to be idiomatic and reveals that here τῆς χρείας is an objective genitive (BDAG 1088; cf., e.g., Abbott 1897: 143; Gnilka 1971: 238; Hoehner 2002: 630). Job is describing how generous he used to be before he was afflicted with his many losses and explains that “when any stranger approached to ask alms, he was required to be fed at my table before he would receive his need [πρὶν λαβεῖν τὴν χρείαν, prin labein tēn chreian]” (T. Job 10.3; OTP 1:843). The stranger surely was not made needier but had his need met. Paul’s meaning here is similar: the goal of the good speech that is to proceed from the believer’s mouth is edification where such edification is needed. Paul may be thinking in particular of the sort of verbal edification that happens when apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers, and the saints they equip exercise their various roles in verbal ways “for the building up of the body of Christ” (4:12; cf. 4:16).

The ultimate purpose for this beneficial speech is that “it might give grace [δῷ χάριν, dō charin] to those who hear.” In ancient Greek literature generally, the expression χάριν δοῦναί τινι (charin dounai tini) could mean simply “to do a favor for someone” (LSJ 1979), and some interpreters have thought that the similar expression here has the same force: good speech is beneficial to the person who hears it—it does them a favor (e.g., Lincoln 1990: 306). In Ephesians, however, the expression “give grace to” has a specific theological meaning: it refers to a gift that enables the recipient to accomplish the task God has given them (3:2, 7, 8; 4:7). Since Paul has just spoken of building up another where the need exists, it seems probable that this purpose clause carries the thought even further and speaks of enabling needy people to function in the way God intended them to function in the body of Christ (cf. 4:16).

[4:30] Paul’s next admonition begins with καί (kai, and), linking it closely with what he has just said and providing an additional motivation for the immediately preceding admonition. Edifying rather than useless and putrid communication should proceed from the mouths of those who are in Christ not only to give the hearer grace but also because otherwise they “grieve the Holy Spirit of God.” The way Paul phrases this (μὴ λυπεῖτε τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον τοῦ θεοῦ, mē lypeite to pneuma to hagion tou theou) is close to Isa. 63:9–10. There the prophet says that God’s people, whom he had redeemed, have nevertheless “rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit” (ESV). The LXX has παροξύνω (paroxynō, provoke, irritate [LSJ 1343; LEH 473]) at this point, but Paul has λυπέω (lypeō, grieve, vex [LSJ 1065]), a word whose semantic range more accurately matches the underlying Hebrew term עָצַב (rebuke, be worried, grieve, hurt someone’s feelings [HALOT 1:864]). Paul’s word choice hints that he had the Isaiah passage in mind, perhaps in Hebrew, as he dictated these words (cf. Moritz 1996a: 92).

This impression receives confirmation from Paul’s next clause, “by which you were sealed [ἐσφραγίσθητε, esphragisthēte] for the day of redemption [ἀπολυτρώσεως, apolytrōseōs].” The “day of redemption” is the future day when those who have rebelled against God will meet with his wrath (5:6; cf. 2:2) and God’s own people will both experience deliverance and receive their promised inheritance (1:14; cf. Luke 21:28; Rom. 8:23). There is a clear echo here of the conclusion to the opening benediction, where Paul has praised God that his readers have heard and believed the gospel and so have been sealed for redemption by the Holy Spirit (1:13–14). Paul now implies that they should not grieve the one who has sealed them by speaking unedifying, foul words.

Just as in the context of Isa. 63:10, then, Paul’s readers are God’s redeemed people, who can make the Holy Spirit sad by engaging in conduct inconsistent with their status as God’s people. What in Isaiah was a tragic account of how Israel had behaved toward the God who had redeemed them has for Paul become an admonition not to follow in the path of God’s ancient people (Schnackenburg 1991: 209; O’Brien 1999: 347–48; Thielman 2007: 826). Paul does not point this out explicitly to his readers, as he has in 1 Cor. 10:1–13 (Schnackenburg 1991: 209; O’Brien 1999: 347), and so he may not expect them to make the connection to Israel themselves, but it seems likely that this connection at least informs his own thinking at this point (Thielman 2007: 826).

[4:31–32] Admonitions about speech are often coupled with admonitions about anger in the exhortatory literature of ancient Judaism (e.g., Prov. 15:1–4; 29:11; Sir. 27:4–28:26; James 1:19–20), and so it is not surprising that Paul moves from a general admonition not to engage in foul speech to a specific admonition about anger. For the fourth time in 4:25–5:2, Paul follows the threefold pattern of (1) a negative exhortation (v. 31) and (2) its positive counterpart (v. 32a) followed by (3) a motivation clause (v. 32b; cf. vv. 25, 28, 29).

Some have thought that his list of five vices in the negative exhortation (v. 31) describes five increasingly intense stages of anger, from the inward emotion of “bitterness” (πικρία, pikria) to the first burnings of “wrath” (θυμός, thymos) to “resentment” (ὀργή, orgē) to “yelling” (κραυγη, kraugē) to “slander” (βλασφημία, blasphēmia; e.g., Eadie 1883: 357–58; Schnackenburg 1991: 211; cf. Herm. Mand. 5.2.4; Origen [Heine 2002: 203]). The early Stoic philosopher Chrysippus made fine distinctions between various types of anger and implied that one form of anger develops into another. He said, for example, that ὀργή was the desire for revenge, θυμός was its first manifestation, and πικρία its immediate outburst (SVF 3:395–97). Much later, the Stoic Seneca (Ira 1.4.2) admitted that the Latin vocabulary of anger was poorer than the Greek, but he was still able to produce a list of eight distinct kinds (cf. W. V. Harris 2001: 55). Pseudo-Phocylides (63–64), a Hellenistic Jew of roughly Paul’s time, thought that “wrath” (θυμός) and “anger” (ὀργή) could bring about “madness” (μανίη, maniē) and “fury” (μῆνις, mēnis), and the first- or second-century Christian who produced the Shepherd of Hermas claimed that “from thoughtlessness [ἀφροσύνης, aphrosynēs] comes bitterness [πικρία], from bitterness wrath [θυμός], from wrath anger [ὀργή], and from anger fury [μῆνις]” (Herm. Mand. 5.2.4, my trans.).

Paul probably does not have such distinctions in mind. All five words in his list, including “bitterness” (πικρία; Rom. 3:14; BDAG 813), can refer to angry verbal abuse, and the admonition to avoid foul communication in the immediate context implies that verbally expressed anger is Paul’s primary concern.[10] “Wrath” (θυμός) and “anger” (ὀργή) are probably synonymous here, just as they often are in ancient Jewish literature (e.g., Pss. 2:5 LXX; 6:2 LXX, MT [6:1 Eng.]; 36:8 LXX [37:8 MT, Eng.]; Prov. 27:4 LXX; Pss. Sol. 2.23; Ps.-Phoc. 63–64).[11] Paul’s list, then, is an elaborate way of describing angry verbiage, not a taxonomy of anger or an outline of its psychological development.

The concluding phrase “together with all κακία [kakia]” describes the inner attitude from which these forms of verbal abuse arise. Κακία is “a mean-spirited or vicious attitude or disposition” (BDAG 500) and is frequently used in contexts where vicious speech is a concern (e.g., Col. 3:8; 1 Pet. 2:1; 1 Clem. 35.8).

Let all this, Paul says, “be removed” (ἀρθήτω, arthētō). The command is in the aorist tense, and this sets it apart from the other ten imperatives in 4:25–32, all of which are in the present tense (Hoehner 2002: 636). This change in tense underlines the contrast between the former conduct of Paul’s readers as unbelievers and the conduct that should now characterize their lives (cf. BDF §337).

In contrast (δέ, de, but) to the malice and angry verbiage of the preceding negative exhortation, Paul’s audience should be “kind” (χρηστοί, chrēstoi) and “compassionate” (εὔσπλαγχνοι, eusplanchnoi) to each other (v. 32a). God has united believers with the risen Christ, according to 2:6–7, so that he might forever show them “the surpassing wealth of his grace by kindness [χρηστότης, chrēstotēs].” The term χρηστοί here recalls this overwhelming, undeserved benevolence of God toward his people despite the sin, transgression, and rebellion they had displayed toward him (2:1–3).[12] The adjective εὔσπλαγχνοι appears in only one other place in the NT (1 Pet. 3:8), but in the Jewish theology of the time, God could be described as εὔσπλαγχνος since he was willing to show χρηστότης even to one whose sins were “more in number than the sands of the sea” (Pr. Man. 7, 9–11 [Odes 12:7, 9–11 LXX]). By the vocabulary he chose at the beginning of this admonition, then, Paul already hinted that he wanted his audience to imitate the character of the God whose graciousness to sinners he has described in 2:1–10.

He makes the theme of the imitation of God more explicit in the motivation clause of this admonition. His readers are to forgive (χαρίζομαι, charizomai) each other just as God in Christ has forgiven (χαρίζομαι) all believers. When Paul spoke of God’s forgiveness of transgressions through the death of Christ in 1:7, he used the noun ἄφεσις (aphesis). His use of χαρίζομαι here may have been intentionally designed to recall the language of God’s lavish grace (χάρις, charis) in Christ in 2:5, 7, and 8 (cf. 4:29).[13]

[5:1–2] Some commentators believe that the οὖν at the beginning of this new admonition signals the start of a new section, as it did in 4:1 and 17 (e.g., Hoehner 2002: 643–44). Others think that it merely links the present admonition to the previous one since both contain the imperative γίνεσθε (ginesthe, be): the imitation of God is a consequence of being kind in the way that God is kind to forgive people in Christ (e.g., Lincoln 1990: 310).

Probably, however, a third, less popular interpretation is correct. The οὖν signals that Paul is now drawing his admonitions in 4:25–32 to a close by stating clearly the principle he has been developing. The previous section has ended with the statement that his readers’ re-creation in God’s image should motivate their behavior (4:24), and the new section began with a διό (dio, therefore) showing that Paul intended to explain what this meant with specific examples (4:25). Now at the close of this section, Paul summarizes his admonitions by returning to the thought that, in their behavior, his readers should be “imitators” (μιμηταί, mimētai) of God.[14]

The notion of imitating God was common in Hellenistic ethics, including Hellenistic Jewish ethics, and that tradition may exercise some influence on Paul at this point. As the additional note explains, however, the primary sources of the idea are probably Paul’s own concept of the church as a human being created in God’s image (2:10, 15; 4:24; cf. Gal. 6:15; 2 Cor. 5:17) and the frequent OT notion that Israel should pattern its behavior after God’s character.

Specifically, Paul’s readers should be imitators of the love of God and of Christ for them. This is the first mention of love since the end of the last major section of the letter (4:15–16), and here it has a summarizing quality. Speaking the truth (4:25), working hard to give to the needy (4:28), using edifying speech that equips others to do the work that God has given them to do (4:29), and being kind, compassionate, and forgiving (4:32)—these are all expressions of love.

Paul’s reference to his readers as τέκνα ἀγαπητά (tekna agapēta, beloved children) probably alludes to their own experience of God’s adoption (1:5) and love (2:4; 3:17, 19; 5:2, 25) that forms such an important theme in the letter. God’s richly merciful, gracious, and forgiving love for them, so unconditional that he decided before he created the world to show it to them, should provide the pattern for their own relationships with one another (cf. 1 John 4:11).[15]

Similarly, his readers should “walk [περιπατέω, peripateō] in love even as [καθὼς καί, kathōs kai] Christ loved.” Paul’s use of the verb περιπατέω for the first time since 4:17 brings this section of his exhortation to a close and forms a positive counterpart to the admonition there that his readers should “no longer walk [περιπατέω] as [καθὼς καί, kathōs kai] the Gentiles walk in the futility of their mind” (4:17). In a way similar to the movement from 2:1–3 to 2:10, Paul has taken his audience from the futility, darkness, estrangement, ignorance, hard-heartedness, and despair of Gentile life apart from Christ (4:17–19) to a life of kindness, compassion, forgiveness, and love in Christ (4:32–5:2).

Paul’s next clause spells out what Christ’s love has entailed.[16] Christ expressed his love for us when παρέδωκεν ἑαυτὸν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν (paredōken heauton hyper hēmōn, he gave himself for us). The idea that Christ’s death was “in the place of” others or “for” others goes back to Jesus himself (Mark 10:45; 1 Cor. 11:24). By the time of Paul, the proposition that Christ died “for our sins [ὑπὲρ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν, hyper tōn hamartiōn hēmōn] according to the scriptures” had already become part of the standard theological instruction handed down to new converts (1 Cor. 15:3). “The scriptures” in view are probably various parts of Isa. 53 LXX, where “the verb paradidonai appears three times for the surrendering of the servant of God and is twice related to ‘our sins’ (53:6, 12)” (Hengel 1981: 36). It is not surprising, then, that Paul often used παραδίδωμι (or δίδωμι) in connection with Christ’s death “because of our transgressions” or “for us,” sometimes emphasizing God’s role in giving Jesus over to death for believers (Rom. 4:25; 8:32), and sometimes emphasizing that Jesus gave “himself” over to death (Gal. 1:4; 1 Tim. 2:6; Titus 2:14; Gal. 2:20; Eph. 5:25).[17] Paul could expect his readers, who were familiar with the catechetical traditions concerning Jesus (4:20–21), to know that this traditional language speaks of the atoning nature of Christ’s death.

Here, however, Paul emphasizes Christ’s own willingness—a willingness that arose out of his love—to give himself over to death to atone for the sins of God’s people (cf. Gal. 2:20). This emphasis is visible not only in Paul’s use of the reflexive pronoun (“he gave himself”) but also in the metaphorical statement that Christ gave himself “as an offering [προσφοράν, prosphoran] and sacrifice [θυσίαν, thysian] to God, for a fragrant aroma [ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας, osmēn euōdias].” The curious phrase “for a fragrant aroma” was an OT idiom for God’s acceptance of a sacrifice because of the sincerity and wholeheartedness of the worshiper (Sarna 1989: 59, 356; 1991: 259; cf. Lev. 26:31; Ps. 40:6–8; Amos 5:21–24; Jdt. 16:16). Paul understood this clearly and so could refer to the gifts that the Philippians sent to help him in prison as a “fragrant aroma” (ὀσμὴ εὐωδία; Phil. 4:18)—the motivation behind them was sincere (Phil. 4:14, 17), and so they were an “acceptable sacrifice [θυσία, thysia], pleasing to God.” Here in Eph. 5:2, then, Paul says that Christ stepped forward willingly, out of his love for God’s people, to sacrifice himself and atone for their sins. This, Paul tells his audience, is how they should live in their day-to-day relationships with one another.

Summary

The love of God and the love of Christ provide the models for individuals within the church to follow in their relationships with one another. The specific ethical instructions of 4:25–32 are practical examples of how the church, as God’s re-created humanity, can fulfill the mandate implied in its creation in God’s image (4:24) and in its status as the body of Christ (4:13–16). The love of believers for one another should imitate the richly gracious and self-sacrificing nature of God’s love in Christ for them.



Additional Notes

4:28. The phrase ταῖς ἰδίαις χερσὶν τὸ ἀγαθόν ([working] what is good with his own hands) appears in a range of Alexandrian (א, A, 81), Western (D, F, G), and particularly valuable minuscule manuscripts (e.g., 256, 263), but a number of deviations from this form of the text appear in the manuscript tradition. A few minuscule manuscripts of a primarily Byzantine text type place τὸ ἀγαθόν at the front of the expression and so take the emphasis off the thief’s hands and place it on the good that the thief now performs. Some Alexandrian and Western manuscripts, including the early witnesses 𝔓46 and B, and perhaps including 𝔓49 (whose text is damaged at this point), do not have ἰδίαις and so speak more concisely of working what is good “with his hands.”[18] Some Alexandrian minuscule manuscripts (6, 33, 1739) have no reference at all to the former thief’s hands and so speak even more concisely of the former thief simply working τὸ ἀγαθόν (the good). Several other minuscule manuscripts (323, 326, 614, 630, 945) have the reformed thief working τὸ ἀγαθὸν ταῖς χερσίν (what is good with his hands); the relatively late uncials L and Ψ also have this reading. The wordiest variation appears in 629 and a few other manuscripts as ἐν ταῖς χερσὶν αὐτοῦ τὸ ἀγαθόν ([working] what is good with his hands).

Lincoln considers the possibility that a scribe introduced the wording of 1 Cor. 4:12 (ἐργαζόμενοι ταῖς ἰδίαις χερσίν) into the more-concise form of the text, but correctly concludes against that theory. Not only does the reading ταῖς ἰδίαις χερσὶν τὸ ἀγαθόν have early and geographically diverse manuscript support, but also at least four of the variations seem to be attempts at improving the style of the expression by omitting ἰδίαις and so making the text less redundant.

4:29. Already in the late fourth century, Jerome had observed that the Latin translations of Ephesians available to him read ad aedificationem fidei (for building up the faith) in 4:29. This rendering deviated widely from πρὸς οἰκοδομὴν τῆς χρείας (for building up the need), which he found in his Greek text (Westcott 1906: 74; Heine 2002: 199). The reading πίστεως (faith) appears instead of χρείας (need) in the Latin-Greek bilingual manuscripts D, F, and G and stands behind a number of other Western witnesses to the text. Jerome thought that the Latin translators had altered the text to make it sound better, but the problem probably lies with the conceptual difficulty of the expression πρὸς οἰκοδομὴν τῆς χρείας. At some point a copyist of the Greek (or perhaps a Latin translator) found this expression incomprehensible and changed it to the more intelligible thought of building up the faith.

4:32. The textual tradition of 4:32, like that of 5:2 (see below), oscillates between the first- and the second-person-plural pronouns. The strength of the witnesses on either side is fairly evenly divided, with strong Alexandrian (𝔓49(vid), B, Ψ, 33, 1739), Western (D), and Byzantine (most) support for ἡμῖν, and strong Alexandrian (𝔓46, א, A, P, 6, 81, 326) and Western (F, G) support for ὑμῖν. The strengths of the internal considerations are also evenly divided. The second-person plural dominates the discourse in 4:25–5:1, but general expressions of what Christ has done for believers in the NT are typically in the first-person plural (Lincoln 1990: 293; Best 1998: 463). A scribe, therefore, might have either conformed the text to the surrounding context (by changing ἡμῖν to ὑμῖν) or conformed the text to the traditional style of similar sayings (by changing ὑμῖν to ἡμῖν). In the end, the evidence slightly favors ἡμῖν for two reasons: (1) the witness to it has a slightly larger geographical spread (Hoehner 2002: 640n2), and (2) precedent for it appears in 4:25 and 5:1–2, where Paul also oscillates between the second and the first person (pace Lincoln 1990: 293; Best 1998: 463; Metzger 1994: 538).

5:1. Elsewhere Paul speaks of the imitation of other churches (1 Thess. 1:7; 2:14), of himself (2 Thess. 3:7, 9; 1 Cor. 4:16; Phil. 3:17; cf. 4:9), of Christ (Phil. 2:4–11; Rom. 15:1–3, 5), and of himself and Christ (1 Thess. 1:6; 1 Cor. 10:32–11:1), but this is the only reference in the Pauline literature to the imitation of God (cf. Michaelis, TDNT 4:666–73). Indeed, the express command to “imitate God” or to be “imitators of God” never appears elsewhere in either the OT or NT.

The notion of imitating God was a major theme in Plato, who uses the verb μιμέομαι to explain how human beings, who exist in the real world, can be assimilated to God, who exists in the world of ideas. This was primarily a mental exercise—“no more than reflection on the image of the god retained in the memory,” as Michaelis puts it (TDNT 4:661)—but occasionally Plato developed the idea of assimilation to God in an ethical direction. People should flee from the earthly realm, he says, where evils hover in the air and should “become like God [ὁμοίωσις θεῷ] as far as possible; and to become like God is to become righteous and holy [δίκαιον καὶ ὅσιον] and wise” (Plato, Theaet. 176a–b, trans. Fowler 1921; cf. Eph. 4:24).[19] These ideas reappear in Hellenistic philosophers and moralists in later years (e.g., Epictetus [Arrian, Epict. diss. 2.14.12]), including first-century Hellenistic Jewish philosophers such as Philo (Flight 63; Moses 1.158; Decalogue 51; Spec. Laws 4.73, 188; Virtues 168), who was heavily influenced by Plato on this point (Flight 63).[20]

This tradition may stand somewhere behind Paul’s use of μιμηταί here, but it is far more likely that his use of the imitation of God as a source for ethics is derived from two other concepts: the idea that the church forms a newly created human being and the OT notion of the ethical imitation of God.

First, in this letter Paul has already developed the idea that his readers, as objects of God’s mercy and grace, form a new human creation (2:10, 15), and in 4:24 he has explicitly developed the idea of creation in God’s image as a motivation for ethical behavior.

Second, in the OT, God’s character and behavior are important sources for ethical instruction. God tells his people to “be holy, for I am holy” (Lev. 11:44–45; cf. 19:2; 20:26); Israel’s release of slaves after six years of servitude is to reflect the generosity of God toward Israel when they were slaves (Deut. 15:12–15; cf. 5:15); and Israel is told to “love the stranger” just as God does (Deut. 10:17–19; cf. Houston 2007: 8–11). It is true that Paul’s term here (μιμητής) does not occur in the LXX, but since Paul has been in such close touch with the OT in the letter so far, it seems likely that the OT’s own concept of the ethical imitation of God would have informed his thinking at this point.

5:2. Just as with 4:32, the witnesses to the text of 5:2 sometimes use the first-person-plural pronoun and sometimes the second-person-plural pronoun. There is variation in both occurrences of the pronoun in this verse, and the decision about which pronoun to read needs to consider the evidence in both instances together. In the second occurrence, the evidence clearly favors ἡμῶν over ὑμῶν: the only important witnesses that read ὑμῶν are B and 1175, and both are of the same text type (Alexandrian). If ἡμῶν is the correct reading in this second occurrence of the pronoun, however, then it is likely that the first occurrence of the pronoun should also be the first-person ἡμᾶς. Despite the presence of ὑμᾶς in some impressively early manuscripts (א, A, B), it is unlikely that the original text would change pronouns in such close proximity to each other, especially since they are in clauses joined to each other by καί (Metzger 1994: 538).





IX. A Reminder of How to Live as New Human Beings (4:17–5:2)

X. Avoiding and Transforming the Deeds of Darkness (5:3–14)

XI. Wise Conduct within the Household (5:15–6:9)

XII. Standing against the Strategies of the Devil (6:10–20)


X. Avoiding and Transforming the Deeds of Darkness (5:3–14)

Paul continues his concrete ethical instruction but does so in a new form in this section. Whereas the previous section (4:17–5:2) is bound together by the themes of changing the clothing of one’s behavior (4:22, 24–25) and imitating God or Christ (4:20, 24, 32; 5:1–2), here in 5:3–14 those themes fall into the background. Instead, the ethical landscape is dominated by consideration of what is shameful and what is fitting (5:3–4), what is hidden in darkness and what is light (5:8–14). The style of the new passage is also different (Lincoln 1990: 317). In 4:25–5:2 Paul telegraphs his ethical concerns in seven brief statements with few connecting conjunctions. Here the concern throughout is with two vices—sexual immorality and greed—and Paul’s admonitions concerning these vices are organized in threes. Three terms describe the two vices of sexual immorality and greed, three words describe immoral speech, and three words describe the people who engage in sexual immorality and greed (5:3–5). This trio of sinful trios is counterbalanced first by “thanksgiving” (5:4) and then by a trio of virtues: “goodness,” “righteousness,” and “truth” (5:9).

Despite these differences from the previous section, this new section also continues the concerns of the previous exhortation (4:17–5:2). Just as that section contrasted the old way of life of the letter’s readers with their new way of life and did so by reminding them of their conversion (4:17–25), so here Paul sets up a sharp contrast between the existence of his readers as “holy people” (5:3) and both the world outside their group (5:7, 11) and their own former existence as unbelievers (5:8). They are to have no partnership with the sexually immoral and greedy (5:7), he says, and are not to share in their behavior (5:11). Paul’s readers were once darkness, but now they are light since they are “in the Lord” (5:8).

The passage has two sections (Schnackenburg 1991: 216; O’Brien 1999: 358). The first section (5:3–7) focuses on sexual immorality and greed as vices to avoid at all costs (5:3–5); it concludes with a warning both against anyone who might teach otherwise and against associating closely with the disobedient who engage in these sins (5:6–7). The second section (5:8–14) supplies the reason why such close alliances are wrong and develops its explanation by using the metaphor of light. Light and darkness are incompatible with each other (5:8).[1] Light bears the virtues of goodness, righteousness, and truth and tries to find out what pleases the Lord (5:9–10). It exposes the darkness, making visible what the darkness tries to hide (5:11b–13). This active element in the light also transforms the darkness, making it light (5:14a), just as Jesus shines on those in the sleep of death and awakens them (5:14b).

The precise target of Paul’s warnings here is not clear. Some interpreters believe that the deceivers in 5:6 are false teachers in the Christian community advocating a lenient approach to ethics (Best 1998: 473–74, 483–85), and some think the language of “exposing” hidden and shameful deeds refers to church discipline (Hoehner 2002: 679–80; cf. Best 1998: 492). The quotation of an early Christian hymn in 5:14, then, is intended to urge believers to live in a way that is consistent with their conversion (Hoehner 2002: 687–88).

As the exegesis below spells out, however, it is more likely that Paul’s warnings in this passage are a complex mixture of admonitions both to avoid sexual immorality and greed wherever they occur and to work for the transformation of unbelievers who are mired in these sins. In 5:6, Paul warns against anyone claiming that God will not judge wrongdoing, whether they are believers or not (so correctly, Hoehner 2002: 663), and then in 5:7 he warns against participating with “the sons of disobedience” in their sins. “The sons of disobedience” are probably unbelieving Gentiles, since Paul uses the phrase this way in 2:2. When Paul tells his readers to “expose” the unfruitful works of darkness, moreover, he probably does not refer to erring Christians and their deeds since in the next phrase he says that the things done “by them” in secret are shameful. The pronoun “them” in this phrase refers back to “the sons of disobedience” and so, once again, must refer to unbelievers. This way of reading the passage seems to be confirmed by the quotation from the piece of early Christian liturgy in 5:14b. There a preacher of the gospel calls on people to rise from the dead, and this is most likely a reference to unbelievers whom Paul considers, according to 2:1, to be dead in their trespasses and sins.

In summary, 5:3–14 accomplishes two goals. First, it warns believers not to become ensnared in the sexual immorality and greed that characterize the unbelieving Gentile world (cf. 4:17–19). Second, it calls on believers to shine the transforming light of the gospel on unbelievers and urge them to rise from the dead.





X. Avoiding and Transforming the Deeds of Darkness (5:3–14)

A. Avoiding Sexual Immorality and Greed (5:3–7)

B. From Avoidance to Transformation (5:8–14)


A. Avoiding Sexual Immorality and Greed (5:3–7)

Paul wastes no time before identifying his primary concerns in this paragraph and the next: he wants his readers to avoid sexual immorality and greed, the same sins he identified in 4:19 as especially characteristic of unbelieving Gentile culture. There, however, the sins were connected. Greed characterized the utterly debauched and unclean behavior that marked the desperate lives of unbelievers. Here the two sins are separate, as the “or” standing between the two terms for sexual immorality and the single term for greed indicates (5:3). Sexual immorality is Paul’s primary focus, as the multiplication of terms related to it throughout the paragraph shows.[1]

The paragraph falls into two sections. In the first section (5:3–5) Paul uses three vice lists, each with three terms, to describe the sins his readers should avoid. The first list describes behaviors: “sexual immorality . . . and any uncleanness or greed” (5:3). The second list is devoted primarily to sins of speech, probably speech with inappropriate sexual connotations: “obscenity and nonsensical talk or suggestive witticism” (5:4). The third list describes people who do not merely talk about but also practice these sins: “[every] sexually immoral or unclean or greedy person” (5:5).

Paul offers two motivations for avoiding such sinful activity in this first section of the paragraph. Such conduct is not fitting for those whom God has set apart as his people (5:3–4), and those whose conduct is characterized by these sins have no inheritance in the kingdom of the Messiah and of God (5:5).

In the paragraph’s second section (5:6–7), Paul warns his readers against anyone who might deceive them with “empty words” (5:6a). Although he is not explicit, he is probably talking about anyone, whether an erring believer or an unbeliever, who claims that no harm will come to those who are sexually active outside of marriage or who accumulate wealth for themselves. To the contrary, Paul says, the wrath of God is coming on the disobedient (5:6b), and to participate with them in their sin will mean sharing their doom (5:7).



Exegesis and Exposition

3Now do not let sexual immorality and any uncleanness or greed even be named among you, as is proper for holy people, 4and obscenity and nonsensical talk or suggestive witticism, which are not fitting, but rather thanksgiving. 5For be sure to understand this, that no sexually immoral or unclean or greedy person (who is an idolater) has any inheritance in the kingdom of the Messiah and of God.

6Let no one deceive you with empty talk: because of these things the wrath of God is coming on the sons of disobedience. 7So do not become sharers together with them.

[5:3] Paul begins a new section of his letter with δέ (de, and/but), just as he does in 3:20 and 6:21, but here δέ also retains some of its force as an adversative conjunction (“but”). In his summary of the previous section, Paul has just explained that his readers should “walk in love” in imitation of God and of Christ (5:1–2). Now, he says, they should also avoid the contrasting way of life. He describes this way of life with three lists, each containing three vices (vv. 3–5): the first list describes activities (v. 3), the second list describes mainly speech (v. 4), and the third list describes people who engage in the activities in the first list (v. 5).

The first list of three vices introduces the subjects that will dominate the three lists: πορνεία (porneia, sexual immorality) and ἀκαθαρσία πᾶσα (akatharsia pasa, any uncleanness) on one hand and πλεονεξία (pleonexia, greed) on the other hand. A venerable interpretation of these three vices, going back at least to Origen and Jerome, connects them with one another and claims that the “greed” Paul has in mind is sexual greed.[2] Perhaps, the argument goes, Paul was thinking of coveting another’s wife, a form of greed forbidden in the tenth commandment (Exod. 20:17; Deut. 5:21). Paul’s use of ἀκαθαρσία alongside πλεονεξία in 4:19 to describe the greediness with which unbelieving Gentiles engage in bizarre sexual behavior makes this an attractive interpretation of the three vices. His use of the conjunction ἤ (ē, or), however, to separate the two sexual vices from greed make the connection improbable.[3] Here he is viewing sexual immorality and greed separately, as two distinct vices (cf. 1 Cor. 5:10; De Wette 1843: 145).

Πορνεία could refer specifically to prostitution (e.g., Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Ant. rom. 4.24.4; Gen. 38:24 LXX) or to sexual intercourse with a prostitute (e.g., 1 Cor. 6:13–18; Rev. 17:1–2; 19:2), but also more generally to any sexual intercourse outside marriage (e.g., Sir. 23:22–23; 26:9; T. Reu. 4; 1 Cor. 7:2; John 8:41).[4] In both Hellenistic Judaism and early Christianity it was considered a characteristically Gentile vice (e.g., Wis. 14:12; 1 Thess. 4:3–5; 1 Cor. 5:1; Acts 15:20, 29; 21:25; cf. Eph. 4:17, 19) and was often connected with idolatry (e.g., Wis. 14:12; T. Reu. 4.6; 1 Cor. 10:7–8).

Ἀκαθαρσία, used in a literal sense, means “any substance that is filthy or dirty” (BDAG 34), but sometimes it takes on metaphorical connotations (e.g., 1 Thess. 2:3) that become sexual in contexts such as the present one (e.g., Gal. 5:19; 2 Cor. 12:21; Rom. 1:24). As its use in these other passages shows, the term is broad, referring generally to sexually deviant behavior. Here Paul makes this broad reference even broader with the adjective πᾶς (pas, all), which here carries the connotation “any kind of” (4:19; BDAG 784): his readers are to avoid sexual activity outside marriage and all forms of sexual deviance.

Πλεονεξία refers to “greed” or “avarice,” and although it could be used metaphorically (4:19), it generally refers to acquiring and holding wealth. Jewish and early Christian moralists such as Paul were particularly concerned that wealth not replace God in the lives of believers. At the end of his comprehensive study of greed as idolatry in early Christianity, Rosner (2007: 129) defines the greedy as “those with a strong desire to acquire and keep for themselves more and more money and possessions, because they love, trust, and obey wealth rather than God” (the whole quotation is in italics in the original). Rosner makes a persuasive case that, in practical terms, greed among the earliest Christians amounted to an unwillingness to share one’s possessions with the needy (cf., e.g., Luke 12:13–21; Acts 20:33–35). If this is correct, then here Paul may be saying to the wealthy among his readers what he has already said to the working poor in 4:28: the sort of acquisitiveness that leads the working poor to steal and the wealthy to refuse to give has no place among believers.

With particularly emphatic language Paul underlines how pervasive their avoidance of these vices should be. Sexual immorality and greed, he says, should not even be named (ὀνομαζέσθω, onomazesthō) among his readers. He is not being so pedantic in this comment that he has set up an odd contradiction by mentioning vices he says should not be mentioned.[5] This is instead simply an emphatic way of saying that within the people of God a culture should prevail that is utterly different (ἅγιος, hagios, holy) from the culture described in 4:17–19, where these vices are so common. The expression, then, is not far from other similar expressions in Greco-Roman antiquity of about the same period. “And civil strife does not deserve even to be named [ὀνομάζειν, onomazein] among us,” says Dio Chrysostom after a lengthy discussion of civil strife, “and let no one mention it” (In cont. [Or. 48] 16, trans. Cohoon and Crosby 1971–93; cf. Isocrates, Demon. 15; Quintilian, Inst. 1.2.8).[6]

[5:4] Perhaps his statement that sexual immorality, impurity, and greed should not even be “named” among the holy prompts Paul next to list three vices, primarily of speech, and all of them with sexual connotations (Lincoln 1990: 322; Best 1998: 477).[7] The three terms are relatively rare, appearing only here in the Greek Bible.

Αἰσχρότης (aischrotēs) generally refers to “ugliness” as opposed to beauty (Philodemus, De poematis 1.84.12–13; Artemidorus Daldianus, Oneir. 4.2.40; Athenaeus, Deipn. 14.7.23), sometimes to an ugliness so intense that it seems to be disordered and unnatural (Pseudo-Aristotle, Divisiones [Mutschmann 1906: 55, line 2]; Vita Aesopi [Eberhard 1872: 228, line 4]). In contexts where sexual behavior is under discussion, words beginning with the syllable αἰσχρ- (aischr-) refer to unnatural, or disordered, sexual behavior (LSJ 43), and αἰσχρότης probably has those connotations here. The term does not necessarily refer to speech, but since the context is concerned with speech (ὀνομάζω, onomazō, to name; μωρολογία, mōrologia, foolish speech; εὐτραπελία, eutrapelia, clever humor), Paul probably had in mind not only obscene behavior but also discussing or singing about “ugly” sexual behavior as a form of entertainment. Both the behavior itself and verbal descriptions of it were often present at the banquets of the wealthy in ancient Greco-Roman society (see, e.g., Quintilian, Inst. 1.2.8).[8]

Μωρολογία (mōrologia) is sometimes associated simply with “chatter” or “talkativeness” (ἀδολεσχία, adoleschia) in ancient Greek literature (e.g., Aristotle, Hist. an. 492b), but it can also take on very negative connotations. Josephus (Ag. Ap. 2.115) uses it to describe the nonsensical inaccuracies and lies of the anti-Jewish writer Apion; Plutarch, in his treatise On Talkativeness (Περὶ ἀδολεσχίας), associates it with drunkenness (Garr. 504b). Μωρολογία, Plutarch says, is characteristic not simply of light drunkenness (οἴνωσις, oinōsis), in which people are in some possession of their judgment, but also of heavy drunkenness (μέθη, methē). The context in which Plutarch sets these remarks is that of lavish banqueting. In its context here in Ephesians, where talk of sexual immorality and debauchery is in the air, μωρολογία may also carry connotations of the kind of nonsensical talk that emerges from people in attendance at banquets where drunkenness and sexual immorality were common (P. Schmitt-Pantel and G. Binder, BNP 2:490–98; cf. 5:18).[9]

Εὐτραπελία (eutrapelia) “described a clever wit that was consistently recognized as an admirable talent, and that endeared one to others” (Hultin 2008: 194).[10] Banquets and drinking parties were more lively and fun when people with εὐτραπελία were present (Josephus, Ant. 12.173; Diodorus Siculus, Biblio. hist. 20.63.6). Like most positive qualities, however, εὐτραπελία could be abused. Plutarch says that Cicero took the otherwise “pleasant characteristic” of εὐτραπελία too far “and so annoyed many and got the reputation of being malicious” (Plutarch, Cic. 5.4, trans. Perrin 1914–26; quoted in Hultin 2008: 192–93). The adjectival form of the word, εὐτράπελος (eutrapelos), could describe a profane (σαπρός, sapros) “wise guy,” such as the slave Aesop, whose talkativeness often involved sexually vulgar speech (Vita Aesopi 32; Hultin 2008: 191n173). In the context of Eph. 5:3–4, where the concern is with inappropriate sexual behavior and speech, the term probably refers to the misuse of an otherwise attractive quality: quick-witted, clever humor employed in malicious or sexually vulgar ways.

The terms μωρολογία and εὐτραπελία are separated from each other by ἤ, indicating that they are different from each other (Best 1998: 478). One term is associated with dullness of mind, a dullness sometimes induced by drunkenness, whereas the other term is associated with a quick wit, able to pinpoint precisely the weakness in an opponent that can be mocked and elicit laughter or able to turn an otherwise innocent phrase into a sexual allusion. Whether its source is wits dulled by wine or sharpened by rhetorical training, rude speech of a sexual nature or at another’s expense has, Paul says, no place among God’s people.

Obscenity, nonsensical babbling, and coarse or mean-spirited humor, Paul continues, “are not fitting” (ἀνῆκεν, anēken).[11] The term ἀνῆκεν was sometimes used to refer to a legal obligation, for example, to pay taxes (1 Macc. 11:35) or to honor the king (2 Macc. 14:8), and here it refers to conduct that is proper or fitting in light of the society of “the holy” to which believers belong (cf. v. 3; Col. 3:18; Philem. 8; Schlier, TDNT 1:360; BDAG 79).

Instead of unfitting speech, holy people should engage in “thanksgiving” (εὐχαριστία, eucharistia). Within the NT εὐχαριστία is a distinctively Pauline word: out of its fifteen appearances, twelve are in the Pauline corpus. Wherever the term appears in Paul, the thanksgiving is always directed to God (Best 1998: 479–80; Hoehner 2002: 658). Here Paul may have in mind an attitude of thanksgiving in one’s private prayers (1 Thess. 3:9; Phil. 4:6; Col. 4:2; cf. Eph. 1:16) or the expressions of thanksgiving that characterize Christian worship (cf. 1 Cor. 14:16; 1 Tim. 2:1) and that in 5:18–20 he contrasts with drunkenness. In either case, speech oriented toward God should replace the self-indulgent, self-promoting speech that Paul has described in the first part of the verse.

[5:5] Paul now gives the reason why (γάρ, gar, for) it is so important to avoid sexual immorality, and speech about it, as well as greed. He underlines the importance of the reason he is about to give with the phrase ἴστε γινώσκοντες (iste ginōskontes). Interpreters sometimes take this phrase as an indicative (“Of this you are well aware”; Bruce 1984: 369, 371n23), and sometimes as an imperative (“For certainly know this”; Best 1998: 472, 480). In the two other places where Paul warns his readers that those who engage in certain kinds of behavior “will not inherit the kingdom of God,” he begins his warning with a reference either to what he has taught them before or to what they should already know (Gal. 5:21; 1 Cor. 6:9). If he follows the same pattern here, we should understand the phrase as an indicative (Bruce 1984: 371n23). The imperative mood predominates in the surrounding context (Best 1998: 480), however, and in the few other places in ancient Greek literature where the phrase appears, it seems to mean something like “Be sure you understand this.”[12] That is probably also its meaning here.

The warning that comes next provides an emphatic conclusion to the two lists of vices in verses 3 and 4. Paul now gives a list of three types of people who are defined by the behaviors he has described in the first two lists: the sexually immoral person (πόρνος, pornos), the unclean person (ἀκάθαρτος, akathartos), and the greedy person (πλεονέκτης, pleonektēs). Such people, he says, have no “inheritance [κληρονομία, klēronomia] in the kingdom of the Messiah and of God.”

The statement is similar to Gal. 5:19–21 and 1 Cor. 6:9–10, where those engaged in various vices—including those who practice πορνεία, ἀκαθαρσία, and εἰδωλολατρία (eidōlolatria; Gal. 5:19–21) and those who are πόρνοι, εἰδωλολάτραι, and πλεονέκται (1 Cor. 6:9–10)—also will not “inherit [κληρονομέω, klēronomeō] the kingdom of God.” Three differences between those statements and the one here, however, are important.

First, Paul adds to his mention of the πλεονέκτης (pleonektēs, greedy person) the explanatory comment that the greedy person is an εἰδωλολάτρης (eidōlolatrēs, idolater).[13] Paul also makes this equation in Col. 3:5, where he speaks only slightly differently of “greed” (πλεονεξία, pleonexia) as “idolatry” (εἰδωλολατρία). As Rosner (2007: 159–64; cf. 129) has shown, “idolater” (or “idolatry”) is being used metaphorically in this expression to describe the vice of giving to money the love, devotion, confidence, trust, service, and obedience that in the Jewish and early Christian tradition should belong to God alone. The idea is not simply that “love of money leads to idolatry,” as T. Jud. 19.1 puts it, but that it is, metaphorically speaking, idolatry (Rosner 2007: 16–18).

This sentiment frequently appears in ancient Jewish and early Christian literature. Job says, “If I have put my trust in gold or said to pure gold, ‘You are my security,’ . . . then these also would be sins to be judged, for I would have been unfaithful to God on high” (Job 31:24–28, as quoted in Rosner 2007: 76), and Eliphaz tells Job to make “the Almighty . . . your gold and your precious silver” (Job 22:25 NRSV; Rosner 2007: 79). Philo believed that the first and second commandments of the Decalogue prohibited not only literal idolatry but also the love of gold and silver money, which can be treasured “like a divine image in a sanctuary, believing it to be a source of blessing and happiness of every kind” (Philo, Spec. Laws 1.23; quoted in Rosner 2007: 85; cf. Philo, Dreams 1.179; Drunkenness 75; Abraham 208–24; Rosner 2007: 86). Jesus claimed that it was impossible to serve both God and money as masters (Matt. 6:24; Luke 16:13; Rosner 2007: 166–67). Polycarp (Phil. 11.2) taught, “If a man does not avoid love of money, he will be polluted by idolatry, and will be judged as one of the Gentiles, who are ignorant of the Lord’s judgment” (quoted in Rosner 2007: 155; trans. Holmes 2007).

The greedy person is an idolator, then, because wealth rather than God is the greedy person’s security, and the object of his or her love and devotion. Although Eadie (1883: 375) wrote long before the kind of careful research on this phrase that Rosner provides, he nevertheless pinpoints the metaphor’s meaning precisely: “The covetous man makes a god of his possessions, and offers to them the entire homage of his heart. That world of which the love and worship fill his nature, is his god, for whose sake he rises up early and sits up late.”

The second major difference between Eph. 5:5 and the two earlier passages (Gal. 5:19–21 and 1 Cor. 6:9–10) is the use in Ephesians of the present rather than the future tense to speak of the inheritance from which the sexually immoral and greedy are excluded.[14] Elsewhere Ephesians clearly affirms the future element of the inheritance—the Holy Spirit’s presence is its down payment (1:13–14)—but here the focus is on an inheritance that in some sense presently exists and from which the sexually immoral and greedy are presently excluded (οὐκ ἔχει, ouk echei, does not have).

The reason for this emphasis on a presently existing inheritance becomes clear when we examine the third main difference between Eph. 5:5 and the other two passages. Here we find the expression “the kingdom of the Messiah and of God” (ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ Χριστοῦ καὶ θεοῦ, hē basileia tou christou kai theou) rather than simply “the kingdom of God.” In the NT, talk of Christ’s kingdom is infrequent (2 Tim. 4:1, 18; 2 Pet. 1:11; cf. 1 Clem. 50.3; Mart. Pol. 22.1, 3), and the phrase “the kingdom of the Christ and of God,” with the article and the added reference to God, is unique. This unique expression, then, emphasizes the present reign of the Messiah together with God himself. Paul has already said that after God raised Christ from the dead, he seated him at his “right hand, in the heavenly places” (1:20). Mention of God’s right hand is a clear allusion to Ps. 110:1 MT, Eng. (109:1 LXX), where the Lord seats the king at his right hand and promises him victory over his enemies.[15] In Ephesians, God not only has seated the Messiah at his right hand (1:20), but his enemies are also already beneath his feet (1:22; cf. Ps. 8:7 LXX, MT [8:6 Eng.]): both God and the Messiah, then, reign victorious over their enemies. Although the full benefit of this victory lies in the future (1:14; cf. 1 Cor. 15:24–27, 50–55), there is a sense in which believers presently share in Christ’s victory over his enemies (1:23) and are even seated together with him in the heavenly places (2:6; Best 1998: 482).

Here, then, Paul is saying that because of their present position of victory—seated with the anointed king at God’s right hand—believers should be careful how they live. Those who have an inheritance in the kingdom of the Messiah and of God should not engage in the kind of conduct characteristic of unbelievers, who have no share in the Messiah’s reign (cf. Pss. Sol. 17.26–27, 32, 41; 18.5–9).

[5:6–7] Paul does not want his readers to be deceived into thinking that sexually immoral or greedy conduct will have no consequences for those who engage in it. He has already alluded in 4:14, and probably also in 4:20, to false teaching circulating among believers, and if this false teaching is in the background of 4:20, then it must have supplied some theoretical basis for neglecting the Christian tradition about how believers should behave, a tradition Paul reasserts in 4:21–24 as a corrective. During the period in which Ephesians was written, there were certainly people abroad who called themselves believers but who scoffed at the notion of a future judgment in which the wicked would be punished (2 Pet. 3:3–4; cf. Jude 14–15, 18–19) and taught that believers could behave in any outlandish way they pleased: God was, after all, gracious (Jude 4, 16; cf. 2 Pet. 2:2–3, 10, 13–14, 18–21; 3:3–4).[16] The language of deceit was sometimes used to describe this sort of error (Rom. 16:17–18; Jude 16; 2 Pet. 2:3; cf. Col. 2:4, 8), and Paul may be referring to the same kind of problem here. If so, he was warning his readers against those who called themselves believers but laughed at the idea that sexual immorality, greed, and a little “fun” around the banquet table would fall under God’s judgment (cf. Rev. 2:14, 20; 3:4; cf. 2:2).[17]

God’s wrath, Paul insists, “is coming” (ἔρχεται, erchetai) on those who do “these things.” Most commentators believe that the present tense is used here to refer either to the present outpouring of God’s wrath (e.g., Calvin 1965: 198–99; Best 1998: 486; cf., e.g., Rom. 1:18; John 3:36) or to both its present and its future outpouring (e.g., Eadie 1883: 378–79; Abbott 1897: 152; Gnilka 1971: 250; Barth 1974: 566; Schnackenburg 1991: 221). The idea that there is at least some reference to the present here gains plausibility from the present-tense reference to the inheritance of believers in 5:5 (Hoehner 2002: 664), which, as we have just seen, has both present and future connotations.

The present tense of ἔρχομαι (erchomai, I come) is often used in the NT, however, to refer to a future event (Matt. 17:11; Luke 12:54; 19:13; BDAG 395), and frequently that future event is either the outpouring of God’s wrath (1 Thess. 1:10; Col. 3:6) or the coming of Jesus (John 14:3; 21:22–23; 1 Tim. 4:13).[18] Since Paul has already referred to the Holy Spirit as a seal on those who have heard and believed the gospel, and since we should probably think of that seal as a protection against God’s coming wrath (see the comments on 1:13), it seems likely that here too Paul refers to the coming of God’s wrath as a future event (cf. Rom. 2:5, 8; 3:3–7; 5:9; 9:18, 22; Lincoln [1990: 325–26] comes close to this position).

God’s wrath, Paul says, is coming “because of these things [ταῦτα, tauta].” He is not referring to the “empty words” of the previous phrase but to the sexually immoral and greedy behavior described in 5:3–5. Paul is probably opposing the claim of the “empty words” that God will not pour out his wrath on Christians who are involved in such sins. The “sons of disobedience” who do these things, then, are not believers who struggle against such sins and sometimes fail but, as the use of this phrase in 2:2 shows, are people dead in their transgressions and sins and under the sway of the world, the devil, and the flesh (2:1–3). Their existence is defined by their disobedience to God.

Because God’s wrath will come upon the disobedient, Paul continues, his readers must not become “sharers together with [συμμέτοχοι, symmetochoi] them.” The adjective συμμέτοχος consists of the word μέτοχος (metochos), meaning “sharing in, partner” (BDAG 643), and the prepositional prefix σύν (syn), meaning “with.” It is, then, an emphatic word and indicates the fullest possible participation in something. Its only other use in the NT is in 3:6, where it describes the full participation of Gentile Christians with Jewish Christians in the people of God (see the comments on that verse). Paul’s point here is that fully participating in the worldview and conduct of unbelievers in matters of sex and money is incompatible with membership in the people of God.

Summary

In 5:3–7 Paul continues the concrete ethical instruction he has been giving since 4:25, and here he focuses on sexual immorality and greed. His readers should avoid not only inappropriate sexual behavior but also entertaining themselves with talk about such behavior. Paul may have been thinking specifically about the kind of conduct that seems to have regularly occurred at the banquets of the wealthy in ancient Greco-Roman society. His readers should also avoid greed, which gives to wealth the sort of trust and devotion that should go to God alone. These behaviors, Paul says, are not fitting for God’s people. Those who treat such conduct lightly, whether by the way they live or by what they teach, reveal that they are not really united with Christ the king, who reigns at God’s right hand.





X. Avoiding and Transforming the Deeds of Darkness (5:3–14)

A. Avoiding Sexual Immorality and Greed (5:3–7)

B. From Avoidance to Transformation (5:8–14)


B. From Avoidance to Transformation (5:8–14)

Paul now supplies another reason why (γάρ, gar, for) his readers should not participate in the sins of the sexually immoral and greedy (5:8; cf. 5:5). The whole paragraph is governed by the metaphor of light, and again it falls into two parts, although less obviously than the previous paragraph. The shift from one part to the next occurs with a move from a passive to an active role for the light in 5:11b. In the first part of the paragraph (5:8–11a), the light is passive, simply defining the new existence of Paul’s readers. In the second part (5:11b–14), it is active, exposing, illuminating, and transforming the darkness.

Paul begins the first part by telling his readers that to participate in the activities of the sexually immoral and greedy would be out of step with the basic orientation of their existence. Their existence is as incompatible with this kind of conduct as light is with darkness (5:8). Instead, their way of life should be characterized by goodness, righteousness, and truth (5:9)—a trio of virtues that contrasts with the three trios of vices in 5:3–7. To put it another way, their lives should be marked by trying to find out what is pleasing to the Lord in any situation and refusing to participate in deeds that are wicked and sterile (5:10–11a).

The second part of the paragraph begins in 5:11b, where the metaphor of light takes a different and more aggressive turn. Paul urges his readers to “expose” evil. Although it is shameful even to describe (much less participate in) evil, the light can reveal it for the futile activity that it is (5:11b–12; cf. 4:17–19; 5:11a) and this, in turn, can transform those who engage in evil deeds into light themselves (5:13–14a). Paul supports his argument with a quotation from an early Christian liturgy that speaks of Christ shining on and transforming one who is asleep and dead so that he or she awakens to life and light (5:14b).



Exegesis and Exposition
