8For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of the light 9(for ⌜the fruit of the light⌝ is in all goodness and righteousness and truth), 10trying to find out what is pleasing to the Lord. 11And do not participate in the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather expose them. 12For the things done by them in secret are shameful even to talk about, 13but everything exposed by the light becomes visible, 14afor everything visible is light. 14bTherefore it says,

Get up, O sleeper,

And rise from the dead,

And ⌜Christ will shine on you⌝.

[5:8] In addition to the reason Paul has just given for avoiding sexual immorality and greed (God’s wrath comes on those who do these things), his readers should avoid them because (γάρ, gar, for) participating in these sins would be inconsistent with the basic orientation of their new existence. Paul’s readers “were once [ποτέ, pote] darkness, but now [νῦν δέ, nyn de] are light in the Lord.” They were not merely in darkness but were darkness, and so their entire existence was defined by it. Now, however, they “are light in the Lord.” Their existence is defined by the light because the boundaries of their existence are defined by the Lord.

This is the language of both conversion and ethical instruction. The use of ποτέ and νῦν δέ to set up a contrast between preconversion and postconversion existence was common in early Christian literature (e.g., Rom. 11:30; 1 Pet. 2:10; cf. Gal. 1:23) and is characteristic of Ephesians (2:11, 13; cf. 2:2–4). The contrast between light and darkness as a metaphor for conversion is also characteristic of early Christian literature (2 Cor. 4:6; Col. 1:13; 1 Pet. 2:9; 1 Clem. 59.2) and appears naturally in Ephesians, where unbelievers are described as “darkened in understanding” (4:18), their activities as the “unfruitful works of darkness” (5:11), and the world in which they live as “this darkness” (6:12; cf. Luke 22:53; John 3:19).

The contrast between light and darkness was also used in early Christian ethical instruction. Paul used the metaphor in 1 Thess. 5:4–11 and in Rom. 13:11–14 to make a link between eschatology and ethics. Both passages have verbal and conceptual connections to the ethical teaching in Eph. 4–6:

1 Thessalonians 5:4–11 Romans 13:11–14



* * *





4You, brothers [and sisters], are not in darkness that the day, like a thief, should catch you. 5For you are all sons of the light [υἱοὶ φωτός, huioi phōtos] and sons of the day. We are not of the night, nor of the darkness. 6So then let us not sleep as the rest but let us stay awake and be sober. 7For those who sleep sleep at night and those who get drunk are drunk at night. 8But since we are of the day, let us be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love and the helmet of the hope of salvation, 9because God did not appoint us for wrath but for the preservation which is salvation [εἰς περιποίησιν σωτηρίας, eis peripoiēsin sōtērias] through our Lord Jesus Christ, 10who died for us, so that whether we are awake or asleep we might live together with him. 11Therefore encourage one another, and build one another up, one on one, just as you are also doing. 11The hour to be raised from sleep is already present, for now our salvation is nearer than when we believed. 12The night has advanced, and the day is near. Let us therefore put off the works of darkness and put on the weapons of light. 13As in the day, let us walk with decorum, not in debauched feasting and drinking binges, not in sexual liaisons and excesses, not in division and envy, 14but put on the Lord Jesus Christ and do not make provision for the flesh, for the purpose of evil desires.



* * *





In these passages the darkness-light metaphor mingles with the metaphor of “putting off” certain behaviors and “putting on” other attitudes or behaviors (cf. Eph. 4:22–24), and the “putting on” side of the image is articulated in terms of donning weaponry for battle (cf. Eph. 6:10–17). In 1 Thessalonians, the theme of rescue from God’s wrath on that day is present (1 Thess. 5:9), and both passages articulate the idea that believers, as people of the light, will be kept safe on the final day (1 Thess. 5:4–5, 9; Rom. 13:11). The eschatological tone of the light-dark imagery in Ephesians is certainly more “realized” than in 1 Thessalonians and Romans—the ethical admonitions are based on one’s existence as light rather than darkness, not on identification with the light of the soon-coming day—but as we have just seen in the comments on God’s coming wrath in Eph. 5:6, eschatology is not absent from the Ephesians context; the difference is one of emphasis rather than contradiction.

The difference in emphasis, however, is important. In 1 Thessalonians and Romans the light metaphor moves from the final “day” to believers as people of the “light.” Their behavior as people of the “light” is motivated in part by their reckoning with the events of that “day.” In Ephesians the final day disappears from view after mention of God’s wrath in 5:6, and the metaphor develops in the direction of believers’ existence as light, whether as light itself (v. 8a) or as children of the light (τέκνα φωτός, tekna phōtos, v. 8b). Because they are light and children of the light, they should “walk” (περιπατεῖτε, peripateite) in a way that reveals what and who they are.

Later, in verses 11–14, Paul will use this metaphor to describe the influence his readers should have on the culture surrounding them: since they are light, they should shine on unbelievers, both exposing their hidden and shameful existence and transforming them into light also. The imagery of military armor and weaponry (1 Thess. 5:8; Rom. 13:12) falls away to be used later for a different purpose (6:10–17), and instead of emphasizing the battle to keep oneself free from societal evils, Paul in verses 11–14 will underline the transforming effect that illuminated believers can have on the darkness around them.[1]

[5:9] Paul now inserts a parenthetical comment expanding on the idea that “children of the light” should “walk” in a way appropriate to the basic orientation of their existence. Just as children share their parent’s nature, so the fruit of a plant shares the nature of the plant that produced it (cf., e.g., Sir. 23:25; 27:6; Matt. 7:16–20; Luke 6:43–44; John 15:2–17; James 3:12; Ign. Eph. 14.2; Davies and Allison 1988: 706). If Paul’s readers are light and are children of the light, then they should produce “fruit” appropriate to the light. The step from “children” to “fruit” is natural for someone familiar with the LXX, where children are sometimes metaphorically described as “the fruit of the womb” (Gen. 30:2; Ps. 131:11 [132:11 MT, Eng.]; Mic. 6:7; Lam. 2:20; cf. Luke 1:42; Acts 2:30; BDAG 510). The use of the term “fruit” in an ethical sense is also characteristic of Paul. He has previously contrasted the “works of the flesh” (Gal. 5:19–21) with “the fruit of the Spirit” (Gal. 5:22–23), has spoken of “the fruit of righteousness” (Phil. 1:11), and has described sanctification as the “fruit” that enslavement to God yields (Rom. 6:21–22; cf. Rom. 7:4; Col. 1:6, 10).[2]

Here the ethical fruit produced by a life oriented to the light is “all goodness and righteousness and truth.” Just as the lists of vices in 5:3–5 came in sets of three, so this contrasting list of virtues comes in a set of three.

Ἀγαθωσύνη (agathōsynē, goodness) is an unusual term: it appears in extant Greek literature prior to the Pauline Epistles only in the LXX (Spicq, TLNT 1:3), where it means “goodness, kindness” (LEH 2) and is often used of showing benevolence to others (Judg. 9:16 Vat.; 2 Chron. 24:16; Ps. 51:5 [52:5 MT; 52:3 Eng.]; cf. 2 Thess. 1:11; Gal. 5:22; Rom. 15:14; T. Jud. 18.4; T. Ab. 1.5; Acts Paul 1, line 4). In the LXX the term typically has practical, material connotations. Nehemiah, for example, describes God’s “great goodness [ἀγαθωσύνη]” as his gift to Israel of Canaan with its “lofty cities . . . homes filled with all sorts of goods, hewn cisterns, vineyards and olive orchards, and every sort of fruit tree in abundance.” There, he says, “they ate and were filled and became fat and were nourished” (2 Esd. 19:25 NETS [Neh. 9:25 MT, Eng.]; cf. Eccles. 4:8; 5:10, 17; 6:3, 6; 7:14; 9:18). This practical, active side of ἀγαθωσύνη is probably also behind Paul’s use of it in 2 Thess. 1:11, where he prays that God might fill the Thessalonian believers with “every resolve of goodness [ἀγαθωσύνης] and work of faith in power.” Coupled in this context with resolve, work, and power, the term seems to mean doing what is good.[3]

Here in Ephesians, then, the term supplies the opposite of the greed that features so prominently in the vice lists of 5:3–5. Those who are in the Lord shine as light when they are benevolent toward others, demonstrating their goodness to them in practical ways.

Δικαιοσύνη (dikaiosynē, righteousness) and ἀλήθεια (alētheia, truth) also appear together in 4:24 and 6:14. Although δικαιοσύνη in the Pauline corpus can refer to God’s saving power (e.g., Rom. 1:17) and to the status of acquittal that God gives to the ungodly (e.g., Rom. 5:17; 1 Cor. 1:30; Phil. 3:9), its close association here with the active term “goodness” shows that it refers to “upright behavior” (BDAG 248; cf. Phil. 1:11; 2 Cor. 6:14; 11:15; Rom. 6:13, 16, 18–20; 1 Tim. 6:11; Titus 3:5; 2 Tim. 2:22). Elsewhere in Ephesians, ἀλήθεια seems to refer to specifically Christian truth (1:13; 4:21; cf. 4:24–25; 6:14). Since “goodness” and “righteousness” are ethical qualities here, however, “truth” is probably also used in this way. Paul was probably thinking of behavior that is forthright and honest, just as David conducted himself before God “in truth [ἀληθείᾳ] and in righteousness [δικαιοσύνῃ] and in uprightness [εὐθύτητι, euthytēti] of heart” (1 Kings 3:6 NETS; cf. Ps. 14:2 LXX [15:2 MT, Eng.]).

Jewish and Christian literature from antiquity frequently describes the character of God in terms of these three virtues. God displays “goodness” to his people and to those in need (Judg. 8:35 Alex.; Neh. 9:25, 35; 13:31 [2 Esd. 19:25, 35; 23:31 LXX]; Pr. Man. 14 [Odes 12.14 LXX]; cf. Barn. 2.9), and the twin characteristics “righteousness and truth” are a persistent feature of his character both in Judaism and in early Christianity (e.g., Neh. 9:33 [2 Esd. 19:33 LXX]; Pss. 84:11 LXX [85:12 MT; 85:11 Eng.]; 95:13 LXX [96:13 MT, Eng.]; 118:75 [119:75 MT, Eng.]; Tob. 1:3; Rom. 3:4; Rev. 16:7; 19:2). Behind Paul’s choice of these three terms, then, is probably the theme of the imitation of God that has surfaced more explicitly in 4:24 and 5:1.[4]

[5:10] Paul now picks up his main thought again after the explanatory digression of verse 9. His readers should conduct themselves as children of the light, bearing the fruit of all goodness, righteousness, and truth, “by finding out [δοκιμάζοντες, dokimazontes] what is pleasing to the Lord” (cf. NRSV). Acting in goodness, righteousness, and truth is clearly pleasing to the Lord Jesus Christ, but these are general terms that offer only a broad form of ethical guidance. Deciding what is benevolent, right, honest, and therefore pleasing to the Lord in any given situation is often complicated, and Paul recognizes this by qualifying his imperative to “walk” as children of the light with the participle δοκιμάζοντες.[5] The verb δοκιμάζω (dokimazō) could refer to trying out a new yoke of oxen to see whether they would perform as the purchaser expected (Luke 14:19), to examining religious utterances and claims to determine their authenticity and truth (1 Thess. 5:21; 1 John 4:1; Did. 12.1), and to examining candidates for positions of leadership in the church to see whether they are qualified for service (1 Tim. 3:10; 1 Clem. 42.4). It referred, then, to the “exercise of critical judgment.”[6] Here it refers to the believer’s use of critical judgment to “find out” (NRSV) in any given situation what he or she should do.

This approach to ethics seems to have been a studied aspect of Paul’s theological convictions.[7] Although he certainly handed on to those under his pastoral care a set body of ethical teaching (4:21–24; cf. 1 Thess. 4:1; 2 Thess. 2:15; 3:6; 1 Cor. 4:17; Rom. 6:17), he also intentionally left room for believers to make decisions by using their own renewed thinking. “Do not be conformed to this age,” he told the Romans, “but be transformed by the renewal of the mind that you might exercise critical judgment to find out [δοκιμάζειν, dokimazein] what is the will of God, what is good [τὸ ἀγαθόν, to agathon] and acceptable [εὐάρεστον, euareston] and perfect” (Rom. 12:2). Later he encourages the Roman Christians not to “judge” or “despise” one another over peripheral matters of religious observance. “Let each person be fully convinced in his own mind,” he advises (14:5; cf. Gal. 6:4; 1 Cor. 11:28; Phil. 1:10), and “Blessed is the one who does not condemn himself by what he approves [δοκιμάζει, dokimazei]” (Rom. 14:22). Later still, Paul is somewhat apologetic about the ethical instruction he has felt compelled to give the Romans and assures them that he knows they are competent to decide for themselves how to behave: “But I myself am persuaded, my brothers [and sisters], that you are full of goodness [ἀγαθωσύνης, agathōsynēs], full of all knowledge, and able to instruct one another” (Rom. 15:14). At roughly the same time that Paul wrote Ephesians, he shows the same reticence to command Philemon to treat the slave Onesimus with love (v. 16) and send him back to Paul (vv. 13–14, 20–21). He tells Philemon that he is bold enough to order him to do this but that he prefers instead to appeal to Philemon to do “what is fitting” (τὸ ἀνῆκον, to anēkon; cf. Eph. 5:4) on the basis of his own loving disposition (vv. 7–9, 14; Thielman 2005: 390). In the same way, here in Ephesians Paul urges his readers to use discernment in deciding what is pleasing to the Lord—what counts as benevolent, righteous, and true—in any given situation.

[5:11] Paul now turns to the negative counterpart of the positive command to walk as children of the light. His readers are not to “participate” (συγκοινωνεῖτε, synkoinōneite) in the “unfruitful [ἀκάρποις, akarpois] works of darkness.” This admonition repeats the sentiment of 5:7, where Paul urged his readers not to be “sharers together with” (συμμέτοχοι, symmetochoi) “the sons of disobedience,” whose behavior is marked by greed and sexual immorality (5:3–6). The terms συγκοινωνεῖτε and συμμέτοχοι both begin with the preposition σύν, and this suggests the incompatibility of participating both in the community of God’s people, which Paul has also described with συν- compounds (2:5, 6, 19, 21–22; 3:6; 4:3, 16), and participating in the activities of those who practice the “works of darkness” (cf. Robinson 1904: 200).[8] The basic orientation of the two communities are as incompatible as light and darkness (cf. 2 Cor. 6:14).

The works of darkness, Paul says, are “unfruitful” (ἄκαρπος, akarpos). Like the light, darkness gives rise to activity, but unlike the light, whose activity bears fruit (v. 9), the activity of the darkness is not fruitful (cf. Rom. 6:21). In other words, it yields no profit and has no point (cf. Wis. 15:4; 4 Macc. 16:7; 1 Cor. 14:14; Titus 3:14; 2 Pet. 1:8). The thought is similar to that of Jude 12, where the futility of debauched behavior is also described as “unfruitful”: “These stains on your love feasts [the false teachers] are those who banquet luxuriously together without fear, shepherding themselves. They are clouds without water, driven along by the winds, late autumn trees without fruit [ἄκαρπα].” The description of the works of darkness as unfruitful, then, is part of the theme of the futility of existence in the unbelieving world that Paul has already developed in 2:1–3 and 4:17–19. It stands in utter contrast to the purposeful, goal-oriented existence that characterizes the believing community because of its union with Christ (1:9–12; 2:19–22; 4:11–16).

Rather than participating in such futile activity, the believer’s existence as light in the Lord leads him or her to ἐλέγχειν (elenchein) the unfruitful works of darkness. This term can mean simply to “uncover” something, such as the source of the Jordan River (Josephus, J.W. 3.512), but it was most commonly used to refer to the exposure of something evil (Josephus, Life 339), deceptive (Aristophanes, Eccl. 485), ugly (Philo, Names 198), or illegal (Josephus, Ant. 4.219, 281) that the perpetrator wanted to remain hidden, but that either through his or her own mistake (Josephus, Ag. Ap. 1.4, 253, 303) or through the evidence provided by another (P.Hib. 55; Josephus, Ag. Ap. 1.4) was nevertheless revealed.[9]

If darkness serves as a cloak for the deception, then light can expose it (John 3:20; Clement of Alexandria, Paed. 3.2.6). If fabricated evidence or specious argumentation hides the truth, these can be exposed by good counterevidence (Josephus, Life 360) or a solidly grounded argument (Philo, Prelim. Studies 18). Philo frequently uses this legal sense as a metaphor for the effect of the conscience on those who intentionally do wrong (Confusion 121; Joseph 262; Spec. Laws 1.235; Virtues 206; Unchangeable 128). In a way that is consistent with these more-complex negative meanings, the term can also mean simply “rebuke” or “reprove” and can carry this simple meaning both in the LXX (Gen. 31:42; 2 Chron. 26:20; Ps. 6:1 [6:2 LXX, MT]) and in the NT (Luke 3:19; 1 Tim. 5:20).

The term can also take on positive connotations, however, by referring to the action of pointing out error in order to correct it and put someone back on the right path. The LXX and the NT use the term this way to refer to God’s fatherly discipline (2 Sam. 7:14; Prov. 3:11–12; Wis. 12:2; Sir. 18:13; Heb. 12:5–6; Rev. 3:19; cf. Philo, Prelim. Studies 177), to describe the helpful correction that the wise person could offer to others (Prov. 9:7–8), to depict the correction that one believer could offer others on the basis of authoritative tradition (2 Tim. 4:2 [cf. 3:16]; Titus 1:9; 2:15; cf. Titus 1:13), and to express the reconciling correction that those who were wronged could provide for those who wronged them (Lev. 19:17; Sir. 19:13–17; Matt. 18:5; Lutkemeyer 1946: 221–23). Paul can use the term this way of an unbeliever or inquirer who might enter an assembly of believers at worship and, because of prophecies uttered there, is “exposed [ἐλέγχεται, elenchetai] by all, called to account by all,” has the “hidden things of his [or her] heart revealed,” and is led to worship God (1 Cor. 14:24–25). Here exposure has the positive result of conversion.

Which of these many nuances of the term applies to Paul’s use of it in Eph. 5:11? Since the implied object of ἐλέγχετε is “the unfruitful works of darkness” and not the people who do these deeds, and since he uses the term in connection with the imagery of “light” and “darkness,” Paul probably has in mind the exposure of the deeds themselves as the evil practices they are. He may be thinking of a counterresponse to the “empty words” of verse 6 that are used to justify sexual immorality and greed, or he may be referring to the perspective on unbelieving Gentile behavior that he has articulated in 4:17–19—that its origin lies in thinking that is futile, darkened, and ignorant. In either case, his emphasis falls on exposure: stripping sexual immorality and greed of the attractive veneer placed over these activities by those who practice them and revealing their true colors.

If this is correct, the debate among some interpreters over whether the deeds exposed belong to believers or unbelievers is misdirected.[10] The exposed deeds are simply activities that originate in and are cloaked by the “darkness” (σκότος, skotos) and therefore are characteristic of the unbelieving Gentiles of 4:17–19, who are “darkened [ἐσκοτωμένοι, eskotōmenoi] in their understanding” (4:18; cf. 6:12). That believers can fall into these deeds, perhaps as a result of deceptive teaching (5:6), is assumed by the admonition not to participate in them. It is the deeds, however, that are exposed as evil, not the people who practice them.

[5:12] In 5:12–13 Paul expands on the two contrasting parts of 5:11. He gives the reason why (γάρ, gar, for) his readers should not participate in these deeds in 5:12, and in 5:13 he explains why they should be exposed.

First, then, Paul gives the reason why his readers should not participate in the unfruitful works of darkness. They are so evil, Paul says, that they are shameful even to mention. Does this imply that when believers expose the sins of others, they must not use words but only the contrast of their own good behavior? A number of commentators over the centuries have thought so (e.g., John of Damascus [PG 95:848]; Barth 1974: 570–72; Lincoln 1990: 330), but it is unlikely that Paul’s language has this connotation. Just as with his admonition that sexual sins and greed must not even “be named” among God’s people (v. 3), so here, Paul is exaggerating for the sake of emphasis: he is simply underlining how far out of bounds the behavior of some unbelievers lies (cf. 4:17–19; Quintilian, Inst. 1.2.8). The verb ἐλέγχω, moreover, has a verbal nuance (Hoehner 2002: 680). People are “exposed” when verbal evidence, whether written or oral, is presented against them. The activities that Paul describes here, then, are shameful even to mention for the same reason that those who do them seek to keep them secret: they are especially evil.

The way Paul expresses this draws his readers’ attention not only to the unmentionable deeds themselves but also to those who do them. He says not merely, “It is shameful even to speak of the things done in secret” but also, “It is shameful even to speak of the things done by them [ὑπ᾿ αὐτῶν, hyp’ autōn] in secret.” Actions rather than people have been the focal point since 5:8, and so the sudden introduction of those who do the actions with a pronoun whose antecedent is not immediately obvious is somewhat obscure. To whom does the αὐτῶν of this verse refer? “The sons of disobedience” in 5:6–7 offers the only viable option, since they are the only outsiders mentioned in the context and Paul has admonished his readers not to participate in their conduct, just as he does here.[11] Those engaged in the unmentionable deeds of this verse, then, are unbelievers (pace, e.g., Best 1998: 495; Hoehner 2002: 679–82), people who have no inheritance in the kingdom of God and Christ (v. 5) and to whom the wrath of God is coming (v. 6).

In keeping with the imagery of exposing wrongdoing that would otherwise remain hidden, Paul describes the deeds of these unbelievers as done “in secret” (κρυφῇ, kryphē). Some interpreters have wondered why, if Paul is referring to unbelievers, he speaks of their conduct as done secretly. For example, Best (1998: 495) says that in 4:17–19, 22 the author of Ephesians hints that the conduct of unbelieving Gentiles was “unrestricted and blatant,” so here it would make little sense to speak of unbelieving Gentiles engaging in secret misconduct. Instead, he thinks that errant believers are in view. They are trying to hide their conduct in order to escape notice and “loyal members of the community” must openly expose their misconduct (Best 1998: 495; cf. Hoehner 2002: 681).

Paul is not, however, describing the conduct of every Gentile unbeliever in 4:17–19, 22, and “the things done by them in secret” were probably done in secret either because those who did them were themselves ashamed or because the acts were viewed with such disgust in the wider society that public knowledge of them could damage one’s reputation or position. Paul knew that, although many unbelieving Gentiles behaved shamelessly and with no qualms (4:17–19; Rom. 1:32), others had sensitive consciences that accused them of wrongdoing (Rom. 2:15–16; Engberg-Pedersen 1989: 108) and held to sexual boundaries that they considered disgraceful to cross (1 Cor. 5:1).

The writings of Greco-Roman moralists and philosophers confirm this. Quintilian could criticize Roman elites for holding banquets at which children were exposed to behavior “of which we should blush to speak [pudenda dictu]” (Inst. 1.2.8, trans. Butler 1966–69). Epictetus (Arrian, Epict. diss. 4.9) considered “disgraceful [αἰσχροί, aischroi] words, disgraceful [αἰσχρά, aischra] thoughts, and unseemly [ἀσχήμονα, aschēmona] deeds” to be a burden one should avoid (trans. W. Oldfather 1925–28). The context hints that he is talking about sexual matters.

This moral sensibility of unbelieving Gentiles seems to be the context of Paul’s description of conversion in 1 Cor. 14:24–25. There the prophetic exposure of “the hidden things of the heart” (τὰ κρυπτὰ τῆς καρδίας, ta krypta tēs kardias) in the worshiping community leads to conversion (Engberg-Pedersen 1989: 106–7). That these things are hidden because those who do them consider them to be shameful is clear from the judicial language Paul uses of their exposure: the unbeliever or inquirer who has hidden them “is exposed [ἐλέγχεται, elenchetai] by all, called to account [ἀνακρίνεται, anakrinetai] by all.” The person is convicted and called to account because he or she is aware of violating a particular standard of conduct.

In Eph. 5:11–12, Paul’s attention has not yet turned fully to conversion—it is still focused on exhorting believers not to participate in “the unfruitful works of darkness”—but the similar language of 1 Cor. 14:24–25 shows that he can easily speak of unbelievers as engaged in thoughts or activities that they consider to be shameful and try to hide.[12] Here in Eph. 5:12 the focus is on activity (τὰ . . . γινόμενα, ta . . . ginomena, the things done) rather than thoughts, and this, together with the reference to not even speaking about it, heightens the sense of its offensiveness. Paul, then, has narrowed his focus from a general reference to “the unfruitful works of darkness” (v. 11) to an especially evil class of those deeds, which, as Ellicott (1859: 120) put it long ago, “from their nature and infamy, shunned the light of day and of judgment” (cf. Eadie 1883: 384; Haupt 1902a: 199).

[5:13] The δέ (de, but) signals a contrast that matches the second half of verse 11. Paul now explains further his admonition to his readers to “expose” (ἐλέγχω, elenchō) the unfruitful works of darkness, and—although this is not explicit—he seems to be providing a reason for that admonition. The reason lies in this principle: everything the light exposes becomes visible. A number of commentators attach the prepositional phrase ὑπὸ τοῦ φωτός (hypo tou phōtos, by the light) to φανεροῦται (phaneroutai, becomes visible), which would then yield the slightly more intelligible statement that everything exposed is made visible by the light. This is slightly more intelligible because, “on this construction,” as Lincoln (1990: 331) puts it, “a move is more easily made from light as a reference to believers, which it has been up to this point in the passage, to light as a reference to Christ, which it becomes in v. 14b.” Believers are engaged in the task of “exposing” the deeds of unbelievers (vv. 11, 13a), but now verse 13b opens the possibility that “the light” that makes visible is something other than Christians. The evil that Christians expose is made visible by the light, which, as we will discover in verse 14b, is Christ.

On this reading, the statement is certainly less redundant, and something like this is close to Paul’s meaning, but it is improbable that the phrase ὑπὸ τοῦ φωτός goes with what comes after it (φανεροῦται) rather than what comes before it (ἐλεγχόμενα, elenchomena, being exposed). The preposition ὑπό (hypo, by) with the genitive appears three times in Ephesians, and in its other two occurrences (2:11; 5:12) it introduces a phrase that qualifies the preceding verb. Moreover, the term φῶς (phōs, light) appears again in verse 14a without referring to Christ, so the smooth transition from Christians as light (v. 8), to the possibility that someone else might be light (v. 13), to Christ as light (v. 14b) experiences a fatal detour before reaching its destination.

Paul, then, means that all the hidden and shameful deeds done by the disobedient are exposed by the light, that is, by believers, and so these deeds become visible. In what sense, and to whom, do they become visible? If we continue to interpret this text by means of 1 Cor. 14:24–25, then what becomes visible is apparently the inconsistency between the conduct and the convictions of the unbelievers whose unfruitful deeds are exposed.[13]

[5:14a] Paul next explains why (γάρ, gar) it is important for the hidden sin of unbelievers to become visible: all that becomes visible is light. Some interpreters have found this statement disturbing. Abbott (1897: 156) insists, “A dark object shone upon does not become lux (the English word is ambiguous)” (cf. Eadie 1883: 386–87). These interpreters are then compelled to take φανερούμενον (phaneroumenon) as a middle-voice participle and translate, “Whatever makes manifest is light” (Abbott 1897: 156; cf. Eadie 1883: 387). Now we have the simple idea that light, by definition, is that which exposes darkness. As many others have observed, however, in the forty-eight other uses of φανερόω (phaneroō) in the NT (and one in the LXX), the term never appears in the middle voice, and Paul has just used the term in the preceding phrase in the passive voice. A middle sense here, then, is unlikely in the extreme.

Once again, however, 1 Cor. 14:24–25 comes to the rescue, this time combined with 2 Cor. 4:6 and the reference to believers as people who have moved from darkness to light in Eph. 5:8 (cf. Barth 1974: 574; O’Brien 1999: 372). Paul is speaking here of conversion—of the same transformation that his readers have experienced, according to verse 8. Just as they became light in the Lord, so now the people who stand behind the pronoun αὐτῶν (autōn, them) in verse 12 also move from darkness to light. Just as in 1 Cor. 14:24–25, the exposure of unbelievers by the discourse of believers has the salutary effect of exposing the truth about sin, and just as in 2 Cor. 4:6 God shines in hearts to produce knowledge about himself, and just as in verse 8 Paul has described the conversion of his readers as the movement from darkness to light, so here all that is made visible by the light is itself transformed into light. The term “light,” then, is a metaphor for the believer here as it was in 5:8.

It is true that this understanding of 5:14a would be much clearer if Paul had said πᾶς . . . ὁ φανερούμενος (pas . . . ho phaneroumenos)—“everyone who becomes visible is light,” since by using the neuter expression πᾶν . . . τὸ φανερούμενον (pan . . . to phaneroumenon)—“everything visible”—he seems still to be talking about the “things done” rather than those who do them. The movement between deeds and doers has been fluid from 5:8 to this point, however, and Paul will make clear immediately that he has people in mind when he reverts in his quotation to the language of personal address.

[5:14b] Paul supports his statement “everything visible is light” with a quotation that instructs an individual to wake up from sleep and rise from the dead, and then promises that Christ will shine on him or her.[14] It seems to be a piece of poetry, at least if we measure it by Hebrew rather than Greek standards: a Greek poet would not have started each line with a verb (Norden 1923: 257), and the lines cannot be scanned according to Greek poetical meter (Noack 1952: 52). In Jewish and early Christian liturgy, however, verbs regularly appear at the beginning of a clause, just as they do here (Norden 1923: 257–58),[15] and the parallelism of the first two clauses (“Get up, O sleeper, and rise from the dead”) is reminiscent of the parallelism found in Hebrew poetry (Noack 1952: 52).[16]

Two questions have dominated discussion of this “very unusual formula,” as Norden (1923: 257) calls it. The first is where it originated, and the second is why Paul introduced it with a phrase (διὸ λέγει, dio legei) that seems to indicate he thought it carried the authority of Scripture.

Both problems are solved if the quotation is a paraphrase of some passage of Scripture, and a number of interpreters from ancient times to the present have held various forms of this view. Most of these interpreters think that the passage involved was Isa. 60:1, although some have appealed to Isa. 26:19, a combination of Isa. 26:19 and Isa. 9:2, or even Jon. 1:6.﻿[17]

The very variety in suggestions for the text that Paul was supposedly paraphrasing, however, shows the weakness in the theory. The verbal parallels, moreover, are not close, and, although Isa. 60:1 LXX does urge Jerusalem to “be enlightened” in the second-person singular, all three passages describe the transformation of a corporate entity—the people of God—rather than the transformation of an individual, as Eph. 5:14b seems to do with its second-person-singular imperatives.[18] Finally, as Abbott (1897: 156–57) said long ago, mention of Christ “is fatal to the idea of a quotation” from the OT.

Other ancient interpreters proposed that the quotation came from a previously unknown prophecy, perhaps from Elijah, Jeremiah, or Enoch.[19] Jerome entertained this possibility but, in the end, wisely rejected it (Heine 2002: 223). The variety of names attached to the quotation once again counts against the idea: these early interpreters were probably casting around for an authoritative name to attach to unfamiliar material that they correctly sensed Paul was quoting in an authoritative manner.

In more recent times scholars have tried to locate the origin of the quotation in various ancient religious movements. Reitzenstein (1978: 61–62, cf. 398) suspected that it came from “a very early alchemistic writing” (cf. Fischer 1973: 143–44); Bultmann (1951: 175) thought it was “cast in quite Gnostic terms”; and Strecker (2000: 572) proposed that it was formed “under the influence of both similar Gnostic texts and traditions from the mystery cults” (cf. Conzelmann, TDNT 9:348).

Metaphorical talk of waking from sleep, resurrection from the dead, and enlightenment was, however, part of the religious atmosphere of the Middle East in antiquity and appears in a wide variety of contexts. It shows up in the sort of Jewish contexts where Christianity first flourished to describe, for example, the change that comes over the individual who joins the community of God’s covenant people (1QHa 11.19–22; 12.5–6, 23; Kuhn 1968: 129–30), the one who turns from idolatry to the worship of God (Jos. Asen. 8.10–11; cf. Berger 1995: 303), or the person who repents of long-standing sin (Pss. Sol. 16.1–4; Kuhn 1968: 127). This Jewish context probably accounts for Paul’s use of light/darkness and death/life imagery to describe conversion (Gal. 2:19–20; 2 Cor. 4:4–6; Rom. 6:3–11), and it is probably also the context out of which Eph. 5:14b arose, with its talk of sleep, rising, death, resurrection, and light.

Although the quotation is not directly from the OT, then, it was probably composed within early Jewish Christianity. Its poetic structure, its use of metaphor, its reference to “Christ” (ὁ Χριστός, ho Christos, literally, the Messiah), and its occurrence within Ephesians, a text deeply indebted to the OT—all point in this direction.

If the quotation is not from what we know as the OT, however, why does Paul introduce it as if it carries the authority of Scripture? Paul’s introductory formula makes clear that he thinks the quotation is as authoritative as any text of Scripture. Διὸ λέγει (dio legei, therefore it says) occurs three times in the NT: here, in 4:8, and in James 4:6 (cf. Heb. 3:7, 10; 10:5), and in all these uses it introduces a quotation or paraphrase of Scripture. Philo also frequently used the phrase this way (although most often in the passive voice; see the comments on 4:8 above). In addition, the present tense verb λέγει (legei, [he, she, or it] says) occurs thirty-five times in the Pauline corpus, and in all but three of these instances (1 Cor. 1:12; 12:3; 1 Tim. 4:1) it is connected with the speech of Scripture. The reason for this is not far to seek: unlike most people or texts, Scripture continues to “speak” in the present because it remains authoritative despite its origins in the distant past (1 Cor. 9:9–10; Rom. 4:23–24; 15:4; cf. I. Marshall 1999: 537). Like Scripture, then, this quotation “speaks” (λέγει) to the present.

This should not come as a surprise. Already in Paul’s time Christians were beginning to give scriptural authority to the words of Jesus and some elements of Christian teaching with no direct connection to “the Law and the Prophets and the others that followed them” (Sir. prologue 1–2 NRSV).[20] In 1 Cor. 2:9, for example, Paul signals an authoritative quotation with the words, “even as it is written,” but then cites a text that, despite its echoes of several passages from the prophets, remains otherwise unknown (cf. Best 1998: 76, 497). In 1 Tim. 5:18 he couples a citation of Deut. 25:4 (“for the scripture says [λέγει]”) with a word of Jesus as if the Jesus saying is also Scripture (cf. 1 Cor. 9:14; Matt. 10:10; Luke 10:7; Did. 13.1–2). Perhaps most significantly for understanding Eph. 5:14b, in 1 Tim. 4:1 Paul introduces an utterance about the emergence of false teaching in the last times with the rubric, “The Spirit explicitly says [λέγει]. . . .” There is no obvious link here to the OT, but as λέγει indicates, this Spirit-inspired teaching carries the same authority as Scripture.

What is the origin of this new, authoritative voice? A Spirit-inspired psalm (cf. 1 Cor. 14:26)?[21] A fragment of a baptismal liturgy?[22] A hymn anticipating the imminent return of Christ and the final resurrection of the dead?[23] None of this is clear. Since Paul seems to assume that many in his wide audience will recognize the citation, he is probably not citing the kind of unwritten Spirit-inspired speech that 1 Cor. 14:26 describes. His quotation is a carefully crafted piece of early Jewish-Christian liturgy that was probably widely used in the first century but, like so much from that era, was later detached from its original context (John 7:53–8:11; Acts 20:35; Bruce 1974: 82–83) or completely lost (cf. Luke 1:1; John 21:25).[24]

The quotation appears to envision a preacher of the gospel calling the unbeliever, who is imagined as asleep and dead, to a resurrected life in which the light of Christ “will shine” (ἐπιφαύσει, epiphausei) on him or her.[25] The first two lines (“Get up, O sleeper, and rise from the dead”) recall the language of 2:1, 5–6, where Paul describes his readers as formerly dead in their trespasses and sins and then made alive, raised, and seated together with Christ in the heavenly places. The third line (“and Christ will shine on you”) recalls 5:8, where the light-dark imagery of the passage began, and which describes his readers’ movement from their former existence, defined by darkness, to an existence defined by light.

Paul understands his quotation, then, as a description of conversion, and in this role, it explains the statement that everything illuminated is light. His logic runs like this: The lines from a well-known liturgy tell us that unbelievers should awake to the truth of the gospel and rise from their former lives of sin, and if they do this, Christ will shine his powerful light on them. This is how we know that every unbeliever illuminated by the gospel is transformed into light.

The quotation clarifies that from 5:11b onward Paul has been shifting his admonition from a passive to an active focus. He began by urging his readers not to participate in the works of darkness (5:3–11a), but then in 11b–14a he turned to the exposure of the deeds done by the sons of disobedience. Since the quotation is a call for the conversion of the individual, we now understand that Paul has been speaking of more than simply shaming people by revealing their hidden sins. The exposure of their unfruitful deeds of darkness can lead to their conversion, just as it does in 1 Cor. 14:24–25. They can be transformed from death to life and from darkness to light.

If this is correct, then the quotation makes a rather different point than 1 Thess. 5:4–11 and Rom. 13:11–14, despite the closeness of the language. Whereas in those texts Paul uses the imagery of sleep and wakefulness, light and darkness, day and night in order to admonish believers to be ready for the day of the Lord (cf. Mark 13:33–37; Matt. 24:42; 25:13), here the imagery urges the unbeliever to recognize that the day of the Lord has, in a sense, already come. It is a time for wakefulness, resurrection, and transformation through the blazing light of the Lord’s Anointed.[26]

Summary

Ephesians 5:8–14 accomplishes two purposes in Paul’s argument. First, it supplies a second reason (beyond experiencing the wrath of God) for avoiding sexual immorality and greed. This sort of conduct, Paul tells his readers, is as incompatible with their new existence as light is with darkness. The transformation they have experienced enables them to discern what is pleasing to God in the affairs of everyday life, and so their conduct ought to be marked by generosity, fairness, and honesty.

Second, Paul urges his readers to become agents of transformation for those whose lives are dominated by the darkness and the sterile and shameful behavior that comes from it. They should expose this behavior for what it is by training the light of the gospel on those who engage in it. When the gospel awakens people to the reality of their sinful condition, then Christ shines on them and they too become “light in the Lord.”



Additional Notes

5:9. Some ancient witnesses read ὁ γὰρ καρπὸς τοῦ πνεύματος instead of ὁ γὰρ καρπὸς τοῦ φωτός. Although this reading has the support of 𝔓46 and Ψ (whose text is Alexandrian) and 1912 and 104 (whose text is Western), it appears mainly in late Byzantine manuscripts. Φωτός has much broader support from the Alexandrian (𝔓49, א, A, B, 33, 81), Western (D, F, G), and Byzantine (256, 1881, 1962, 2127, 2464) traditions. It is easy to see, moreover, how a scribe familiar with the expression ὁ . . . καρπὸς τοῦ πνεύματος from Gal. 5:22 could have accidentally substituted πνεύματος for φωτός (Metzger 1994: 540), especially since both here and in Gal. 5:22–23 ἀγαθωσύνη is identified as a fruit.

5:14. Perhaps the strangest textual variant in Ephesians occurs in the third line of the liturgical piece Paul quotes here. Instead of ἐπιφαύσει σοι ὁ Χριστός, some Western witnesses (e.g., D, two manuscripts of the Old Latin, Marius, Victorinus of Rome, Ambrosiaster) have ἐπιψαύσεις τοῦ Χριστοῦ (you will touch Christ). Chrysostom was aware of texts that had this reading, but rejected it (Hom. Eph., hom. 18; NPNF 13:133; PG 62:122). Jerome describes attending a sermon where the preacher assumed the text read “ἐπιψαύσει, that is, ‘Christ will touch you’” (Heine 2002: 224; cf. Robinson 1904: 119n1, 300), and Theodoret’s text had this reading (ἐπιψαύσει σου ὁ Χριστός), although he preferred “Christ will shine on you” (PG 82:544; R. Hill 2001: 2.51). There is no doubt that ἐπιφαύσει σοι ὁ Χριστός is correct, as even these ancient interpreters realized, but how did the odd alternatives to this reading arise?

Several scholars comment that the reading arose from the legend that Adam’s skull lay buried at Golgotha (e.g., Abbott 1897: 159; Haupt 1902a: 202–3n3; Metzger 1994: 540), and this is probably correct. Jerome’s preacher, in an effort to entertain his audience with “a theatrical marvel” (Heine 2002: 224), claimed that when Christ was crucified, his blood and body “touched” the buried Adam. According to the preacher, this fulfilled the prophecy that says, “Awake, O sleeper, and rise from the dead, and Christ will touch [ἐπιψαύσει] you.” The audience was so delighted with this clever display that they applauded.[27] The same link between the legend and the quotation appears in Jerome’s contemporary Epiphanius, but this time with the text of Ephesians quoted accurately (Pan. 46.5.8–9). Perhaps the association between the legend and the text began as we find it in Epiphanius, and then as the legend became more popular in the fourth and fifth centuries (with the help of some creative preaching), the text was actually changed to conform to the legend.





X. Avoiding and Transforming the Deeds of Darkness (5:3–14)

XI. Wise Conduct within the Household (5:15–6:9)

XII. Standing against the Strategies of the Devil (6:10–20)

XIII. A Concluding Commendation and a Final Prayer-Wish (6:21–24)


XI. Wise Conduct within the Household (5:15–6:9)

Paul now provides a sustained description of the wise life of the believer, who lives in the realm of the Spirit. Up to this point, he has admonished his readers mainly through contrast: here is how you once lived (or here is how unbelieving Gentiles have always lived), Paul has told his readers, but your new way of life should look, in contrast, like this (4:17–5:14). Much of the emphasis, however, has fallen on describing the debauched way of life that pagans lead (4:17–19, 22, 25a, 28a, 29a, 31; 5:3–8a, 11–12). After a brief transitional section that continues this antithetical style (5:15–18), Paul moves into an entirely positive description of worship in the Christian community (5:19–20) and life in the Christian household (5:21–6:9). This is the life of wisdom lived within the sphere of the Spirit.

There is perhaps an implied sustained contrast here between the life of debauchery, particularly in sexual matters, that marks the lives of unbelieving pagans and the practices of corporate Christian worship and domestic life. Corporate Christian worship stands in contrast to corporate pagan activities such as banqueting, and the Christian home stands in contrast to the sexual immorality of the surrounding culture.

There was no neat separation between these activities, however, on either the pagan side or the Christian side. As we have seen in the comments on 5:3–14, ancient banqueting was well known for its sexual immorality, both in the bawdy songs and jokes that were uttered and in the activities that were pursued. Christian worship, like ancient banquets, took place in the households of the relatively wealthy and often included a meal (1 Cor. 11:17–34; Jude 12; 2 Pet. 2:13). Both in Corinth and elsewhere, Christian banqueting, from an early date, sometimes assumed a form that looked little different from the banquets of unbelievers, and some “Christians” even supported immoral behavior at such banquets with specious theological arguments (Jude 4, 8, 16, 19; 2 Pet. 2:1–3, 12–13, 18–19; 3:16–17; cf. Rev. 2:14, 20). If any of this lies in the background of the wise behavior in corporate worship and in the home that Paul describes in 5:15–6:9, then he was interested in the clear separation of the practices of the believers to whom he wrote from the symposia, convivia, and drinking parties of the wealthy, which had gained notoriety in the surrounding culture.

Paul’s description of the wise life lived within the sphere controlled by the Spirit can be divided into four sections. The first section (5:15–20) stands apart from the other three sections. It briefly introduces the theme of walking in wisdom and in the sphere of the Spirit (5:15–18). This leads to an equally brief treatment of the kind of corporate worship that results from being filled in the Spirit (5:19–20). In turn, this leads to the main concern of the entire passage: the submission of believers to one another in the household (5:21–6:9). Paul’s treatment of this concern unfolds in the remaining three sections, the organization of which corresponds to an ancient division of the household into three primary relationships: wife and husband (5:21–33), children and parents (6:1–4), and slaves and masters (6:5–9).

The theme of wise conduct within the household binds the entire passage together. In light of the evil times in which believers live, Paul seems to say, they should center their households on the worship of God and on loving, heartfelt submission to one another.
